## 2. Per-provider detail

### 2.1 Anthropic

**Memory tool** — GA (beta 2025-09-29 → GA 2026-02-17). Entire config: `{"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"}`. Client-executes six commands: `view` (`path`, optional `view_range: [start, end]`, `-1` = to EOF), `create` (`file_text`), `str_replace` (`old_str`, optional `new_str` — omit to delete), `insert` (`insert_line`, `insert_text`; 0 = prepend), `delete`, `rename` (`old_path`, `new_path`). The API auto-injects into the system prompt:

> `IMPORTANT: ALWAYS VIEW YOUR MEMORY DIRECTORY BEFORE DOING ANYTHING ELSE. … ASSUME INTERRUPTION: Your context window might be reset at any moment, so you risk losing any progress that is not recorded in your memory directory.`

Published results (2025-09-29): memory tool + context editing = **+39% over baseline** on an agentic-search eval; context editing alone **+29%**; **84% token reduction** on a 100-turn web-search eval that otherwise failed on context exhaustion.

**Memory stores** — beta, `agent-memory-2026-07-22`.

```
POST   /v1/memory_stores                              {name, description}
GET|POST|DELETE /v1/memory_stores/{id}                + /archive (one-way)
POST   /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memories                {path, content}
GET    /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memories?path_prefix=/&depth=0|1
GET|POST|DELETE /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memories/{mem_id}
GET    /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memory_versions?memory_id=...
GET    /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memory_versions/{ver_id}
POST   /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memory_versions/{ver_id}/redact
```

Attach at session creation only (not hot-attachable):

```json
{"resources": [{"type": "memory_store", "memory_store_id": "memstore_01…",
  "access": "read_write", "instructions": "Check before starting any task."}]}
```

Mount slug is display-name lowercased with non-alphanumeric runs → single hyphen; **read `mount_path` from the resource rather than constructing it**. Writes elsewhere under `/mnt/memory/` land in container-local scratch and are lost. Optimistic concurrency:

```json
{"content": "CORRECTED: …", "precondition": {"type": "content_sha256", "content_sha256": "<sha>"}}
```

A version that is the current head **cannot** be redacted — write a new version first. Webhooks exist for `memory_store.created|archived|deleted` (note: `created` also fires when "an Anthropic-operated process… clones one of your existing stores" — i.e. a dream). Individual memories emit no events.

**Dreams** — `POST /v1/dreams` with `inputs: [{type: "memory_store", …}, {type: "sessions", session_ids: [...]}]`, `model`, `instructions`. Status `pending → running → completed|failed|canceled`; `session_id` points at the underlying session so you can stream the pipeline. Key property: **the input store is never modified** — output is a new store you review and adopt or discard. Doc is explicit that instructions steer *synthesis*, not line edits: "imperative directives that target specific lines … generally produce no change."

**Context editing** — `context_management.edits[]`. `clear_tool_uses_20250919`: `trigger` (default `{input_tokens, 100000}`), `keep` (default `{tool_uses, 3}`), `clear_at_least`, `exclude_tools`, `clear_tool_inputs`. `clear_thinking_20251015`: `keep: "all" | {thinking_turns, N}` (Opus 4.5+/Sonnet 4.6+ default to keeping all). **`clear_thinking` must be listed first.** Client keeps the full history; edits are server-side.

**Compaction** — `{"type": "compact_20260112", "trigger": {"input_tokens", 150000}, "pause_after_compaction": false, "instructions": null}`. Min trigger 50,000. `instructions` **fully replaces** the default prompt. Emits a `compaction` content block; everything before it is dropped on subsequent requests. Bill correctly by summing `usage.iterations[]` — the top-level counters exclude the compaction pass. Re-sending an existing compaction block costs nothing extra.

**Skills** — three-level progressive disclosure: metadata (~100 tok/skill, always), SKILL.md body (<5k tok, on trigger), bundled files (0 until read; scripts run via bash so **their code never enters context**). `container: {skills: [{type: "anthropic"|"custom", skill_id, version}]}`.

**Tool search** — GA. `defer_loading: true` per tool (max 10,000 deferred; ≥1 must stay loaded). Vendor numbers: **85% token reduction** (77k → 8.7k), Opus 4.5 MCP accuracy **79.5% → 88.1%**, Opus 4 **49% → 74%**. Deferred tools are stripped from the cache prefix, so **`defer_loading` preserves prompt caching**; discovered tools expand inline in the body. Programmatic tool calling: 43,588 → 27,297 tokens (**−37%**).

**Prompt caching economics** — 5m write **1.25x**, 1h write **2x**, read **0.1x**. Min cacheable: Opus 5 / Fable 5 / Mythos 5 **512**; Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / 4.6 / 4.5 / Opus 4.1 **1,024**; Opus 4.7 **2,048**; Opus 4.6 / 4.5 / Haiku 4.5 **4,096**. Max 4 breakpoints; 20-block lookback. Hierarchy `tools → system → messages`.

**Claude Code** — CLAUDE.md hierarchy (managed policy → `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` → `./CLAUDE.md` → `./CLAUDE.local.md`), `@path` imports (depth 4, external imports require approval), `.claude/rules/*.md` with `paths:` frontmatter for path-scoped loading. **Auto memory** (`autoMemoryEnabled`, on by default): `MEMORY.md` index capped at **200 lines / 25 KB**, topic files loaded on demand, `modified` ISO timestamp frontmatter written on each save. The harness *enforces* the cap: near the limit it reminds Claude to shorten; over it, the write succeeds but returns an error telling Claude to rewrite the index. **What survives compaction**: project-root CLAUDE.md and auto memory are **re-injected from disk**; path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md are lost until re-triggered; skill bodies re-inject capped at 5,000 tok/skill and 25,000 total, oldest dropped.

**Compliance** (feature eligibility table): memory tool **ZDR ✓ HIPAA ✓** (client-side); context editing and compaction **ZDR ✓ HIPAA ✗**; Skills and Managed Agents (incl. memory stores) **ZDR ✗ HIPAA ✗** — "Sessions are stateful resources; transcripts persist until you delete them."

### 2.2 OpenAI

No memory service. The durable-state answer is **Conversations** (indefinite retention, exempt from the 30-day response TTL) plus **Vector Stores** for retrieval. The actual *memory* work — extraction, consolidation, forgetting — only exists in the **beta Agents SDK sandbox**, and it is file-based:

```
memories/
├── memory_summary.md            # auto-injected into the developer prompt at run start
├── MEMORY.md                    # keyword index the agent greps
├── raw_memories/<rollout-id>.md
└── rollout_summaries/<rollout-id>_<slug>.md
sessions/<rollout-id>.jsonl
```

Two-phase generation: (1) a memory model summarizes the accumulated conversation; (2) a consolidation agent rewrites `MEMORY.md` + `memory_summary.md`. `Memory(generate=None)` = read-only, `Memory(read=None)` = generate-only. Scoping is by `MemoryLayoutConfig`, **not by agent name** — same layout + same memory conversation ID means shared memory. Conversation ID priority: explicit `conversation_id` → `session.session_id` → `RunConfig.group_id` → per-run auto ID.

Codex CLI uses the *same* two-file pattern, which is the clearest signal of OpenAI's converging house style. `AGENTS.md` remains static, manually maintained, with a reported 32 KiB silent-truncation ceiling (secondary source).

Session protocol (four methods): `get_items(limit)`, `add_items(items)`, `pop_item()`, `clear_session()`. Backends now include `SQLiteSession`, `AsyncSQLiteSession`, `RedisSession`, `SQLAlchemySession`, `MongoDBSession`, `DaprSession`, `AdvancedSQLiteSession` (branching), `EncryptedSession` (wrapper, TTL), `OpenAIConversationsSession`, `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession`.

`/v1/skills` (create/version/set-default, `files[]` maxItems 500) is **the only OpenAI context primitive with real versioning**, and it's in the spec with no narrative guide.

AgentKit's Agent Builder + Evals + reusable Prompts wind down **2026-11-30** (read-only 2026-10-31); ChatKit survives.

### 2.3 Google

Memory Bank is the most complete managed memory service shipped by anyone. Three interchangeable parents: `reasoningEngines/{re}`, the new top-level `memoryBanks/{mb}`, or shorthand.

```
POST .../memories:generate      # vertexSessionSource | directContentsSource | directMemoriesSource (≤5)
POST .../memories:retrieve      # scope + similaritySearchParams{searchQuery, topK} | simpleRetrievalParams
POST .../memories:ingestEvents  # GA 2026-07-08; streamId + generationTriggerConfig
POST .../memories:purge         # filter (AIP-160) + force (dry-run when false)
POST .../memories/{m}:rollback  # targetRevisionId
GET  .../memories/{m}/revisions[/{rev}]
POST .../memories:retrieveProfiles   # v1beta1 only
```

GA/preview split determined by diffing `v1` vs `v1beta1` discovery docs: everything is in `v1` **except** `retrieveProfiles` and the structured-profile schemas — so profiles are GA-*announced* (2026-07-15) but v1beta1-*served*.

`scope` is one concept doing three jobs, all exact-set-equality (order-insensitive, **case-sensitive**): isolation boundary, consolidation candidate set, and retrieval predicate. From a session source it defaults to `{"user_id": session.user_id}`.

Bank config (`ReasoningEngineContextSpec.memoryBankConfig`): `generationConfig.model` (default `gemini-3.5-flash`), `similaritySearchConfig.embeddingModel` (default `text-embedding-005`; `gemini-embedding-2` only on `global`/`us`/`eu`), `ttlConfig`, `customizationConfigs[]` with `scopeKeys[]` (most-specific-wins, one empty-keys default), `memoryTopics[]`, `generateMemoriesExamples[]`, `consolidationConfig.revisionsPerCandidateCount`, `enableThirdPersonMemories`.

Topics: managed enum `USER_PERSONAL_INFO`, `USER_PREFERENCES`, `KEY_CONVERSATION_DETAILS`, `EXPLICIT_INSTRUCTIONS`; custom via `CustomMemoryTopic{label, description}`, selectable per request via `allowedTopics[]`.

ADK: `BaseMemoryService` now has `add_session_to_memory`, `add_events_to_memory` (delta writes mid-session), `add_memory`, `search_memory`. `preload_memory` = auto-injected at turn start; `load_memory` = model-decided. Note `add_memory` defaults to `memories.create`; pass `custom_metadata={"enable_consolidation": True}` to route through `memories.generate` instead. State prefixes: none = session, `user:` = cross-session per user, `app:` = global, `temp:` = discarded after the invocation.

RAG Engine has a first-class `RagCorpus.corpusTypeConfig.memoryCorpus{llmParser}` — this is the substrate behind `VertexAiRagMemoryService`, and it's raw-transcript vector retrieval, explicitly positioned as the alternative when you want transcripts rather than LLM-extracted facts.

### 2.4 Microsoft & AWS

**Foundry Memory** (preview, `api-version=2025-11-15-preview`) — note you'll run **two api-versions in one app**, since agents use `v1`. Store options: `chat_summary_enabled`, `user_profile_enabled`, `procedural_memory_enabled`, `default_ttl_seconds` (0 = never), and `user_profile_details`, a natural-language steering string used both to prioritize and to exclude ("Avoid irrelevant or sensitive data, such as age, financials, precise location, and credentials"). Tool: `{"type": "memory_search_preview", "memory_store_name", "scope", "update_delay"}` — `update_delay` is seconds of inactivity before extraction, **default 300**. Recommended read pattern: `search_memories` **without** `items` → static profile memories injected at conversation start; **with** `items` → contextual memories per turn.

**AgentCore Memory** — control plane (`bedrock-agentcore-control`) vs data plane (`bedrock-agentcore`) are separate services. Five strategies as a union: `semanticMemoryStrategy`, `summaryMemoryStrategy`, `userPreferenceMemoryStrategy`, `episodicMemoryStrategy`, `customMemoryStrategy`. Steps are extraction / consolidation / **reflection** (episodic only). Prompt override field is **`appendToPrompt`** and the doc warns it *replaces* the default instructions — the name lies. You may not rename the consolidation operations `AddMemory`/`UpdateMemory` or the pipeline fails.

Escape hatches worth knowing: `extractionMode: "SKIP"` on `CreateEvent` stores raw but excludes from extraction; `selfManagedConfiguration` gives you `triggerConditions` (`messageBasedTrigger.messageCount`, `tokenBasedTrigger.tokenCount`, `timeBasedTrigger.idleSessionTimeout`) → SNS → S3 payload → your pipeline → `BatchCreateMemoryRecords`.

Metadata pre-filtering (Apr 2026): `indexedKeys` (`STRING`/`STRINGLIST`/`NUMBER`, **cannot be removed, no backfill**), 9 operators, max 5 filters, AND only. `extractionType: STRICTLY_CONSISTENT` copies a value verbatim and **partitions extraction/consolidation** so records from different value groups never merge.

Namespace hygiene: AWS explicitly says use a **trailing slash** (`/actors/Alice/` not `/actors/Alice`) to avoid prefix collisions in multi-tenant apps.

## 3. Cross-cutting patterns

**Context rot is now measured, not folklore.** Chroma's study (2025-07-14, 18 models, needle-in-haystack variants + LongMemEval at ~113k tokens + repeated-words) found degradation "in surprising and non-uniform ways," that "even a single distractor reduces performance," and — counterintuitively — that **shuffling the haystack and destroying local coherence *improves* performance**. Anthropic's framing: context is a finite "attention budget," and the goal is "the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome."

**The three-way tradeoff is now a four-way one, and every provider picks differently.**

| Approach | Cost | Failure mode | Who does it server-side |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prune** (drop tool results/thinking) | Cheap, invalidates cache from the cut point | Silent loss of detail | Anthropic `clear_tool_uses_*` |
| **Compact** (summarize prefix) | Extra sampling pass, billed | Lossy; irreversible | Anthropic `compact_20260112`; OpenAI `context_management` + `/responses/compact` |
| **Externalize** (write to memory) | Storage + retrieval latency | Staleness, contradiction, poisoning | Anthropic stores, Google Memory Bank, AWS AgentCore, MS Foundry |
| **Defer** (don't load until asked) | Near-free, cache-preserving | Discovery misses | Anthropic tool search + Skills; OpenAI/Codex `MEMORY.md` grep |

Deferral is the underrated one. It's the only strategy with no accuracy tax, and Anthropic's tool-search numbers (85% fewer definition tokens *and* accuracy 79.5% → 88.1%) show pruning the menu improves choice.

**Compaction is not always better than a hard reset.** Anthropic's own harness team: "Context resets worked better than compaction for preventing model 'context anxiety'" — they used clean-slate sessions with a handoff artifact instead. Measured on one build: solo agent 20 min / $9 producing non-functional output vs full harness 6 hr / $200 producing a working app.

**Structured note-taking is the convergent house style.** Independently, four vendors landed on *a size-capped index file plus on-demand detail files*: Anthropic Claude Code (`MEMORY.md`, 200 lines/25 KB, harness errors if exceeded), OpenAI Agents SDK sandbox and Codex CLI (`memory_summary.md` injected + `MEMORY.md` grepped), Anthropic Skills (metadata → body → bundled files), and Anthropic's long-running agent harness (`claude-progress.txt` + `feature_list.json` + `init.sh` + git). The scientific-computing writeup calls `CHANGELOG.md` "the agent's portable long-term memory, acting as a sort of lab notes" and stresses recording **failed approaches and why they didn't work** — negative results are the highest-value memory and the least likely to be re-derived.

**Sub-agent isolation is a memory strategy with a known price.** Anthropic: agents use ~4x the tokens of chat; multi-agent ~**15x**. Orchestrator-worker with Opus 4 lead + Sonnet 4 subagents beat single-agent Opus 4 by **90.2%**; token usage alone explained **80% of variance** on BrowseComp. Subagents return 1,000–2,000-token summaries rather than raw context. In Claude Code, a subagent inherits CLAUDE.md but **not** the parent's auto memory — it gets its own directory via `memory: user|project|local`.

**Code execution as a context filter.** Anthropic's MCP-via-code post reports **150,000 → 2,000 tokens (98.7%)** by presenting servers as a `./servers/<server>/<tool>.ts` filesystem the model navigates, and notes the privacy consequence: "intermediate results stay in the execution environment by default," so PII can move between tools without entering model context.

**Interop does not exist.** MCP has five primitives (tools, resources, prompts, sampling, roots/elicitation) and **no memory primitive**. There is a W3C **AI Agent Memory Interoperability Community Group** (launched 2026-06-03, charter 2026-06-19, 17 participants) referencing IETF draft **`draft-saihm-memory-protocol`** — but be clear-eyed: the group's chair and the draft's sole author are the same person, the draft is an Independent Submission (not IETF-endorsed, expires 2026-11-28), it's blockchain-flavored (ML-DSA-65 signatures, public-chain anchoring, wallet-derived keys), and **no deliverables have been published**. No vendor backing. Treat as noise, not signal.

## 4. What's actually novel — the 8 worth stealing

**1. Immutable version-per-mutation that outlives its parent, plus redact-in-place.** Anthropic memory versions (`memver_...`) belong to the *store*, not the memory, carry a `created_by` actor, and survive deletion of the memory. `/redact` scrubs content while preserving who-did-what-when. Google goes further: revisions carry `extractedMemories[].context` = "the explanation of why the information was extracted from the source content" — the pre-consolidation evidence *and the rationale*. Contrast ChatGPT Dreaming, which has better consolidation and essentially no audit trail. **If you build one thing from this list, build this.** Redact-not-delete is the correct GDPR primitive for derived facts.

**2. `content_sha256` optimistic concurrency on memory writes.** Two agents editing the same memory is not hypothetical once you have background consolidation. Anthropic's `precondition: {type: "content_sha256", content_sha256}` is a two-field solution that turns a lost-update bug into a retry. Nobody else ships this.

**3. Consolidation as an offline job that writes to a *new* store and never mutates the input.** Anthropic dreams: input store untouched, output store reviewable, discard if bad. This makes the scariest operation in a memory system (an LLM rewriting your facts) safe to run, and makes it A/B-testable. AWS and Google both consolidate in place; Google mitigates with rollback, AWS doesn't mitigate at all.

**4. `scope` as one exact-match KV dict doing three jobs.** Google's `scope` is simultaneously the isolation boundary, the consolidation candidate set, and the retrieval predicate — with exact set equality, immutable after creation, and IAM Conditions enforceable per scope. One concept, three guarantees, no drift between them. Compare AWS, where namespaces do the *who* and metadata does the *what* — and AWS has to explicitly warn you not to use metadata for tenant isolation because it's "a security-through-convention model that breaks on any missed filter."

**5. A consolidation *partition key*.** AWS `extractionType: STRICTLY_CONSISTENT` (value copied verbatim, LLM never consulted, and records from different value groups never merge) and Google `metadataMergeStrategy: REQUIRE_EXACT_MATCH` solve the same problem: guaranteeing the merge step cannot cross a boundary you care about. If you have any multi-tenant, per-client, or per-legal-entity dimension, you need this or the LLM will eventually blend two clients' facts into one.

**6. Progressive disclosure with a machine-enforced index cap.** Not just "have an index file" — Claude Code *measures* `MEMORY.md` after each write against 200 lines / 25 KB, reminds Claude when near, and **returns an error** when over, because content past the limit is silently dropped on next load. Skills do the same shape at a different scale (~100 tok metadata → <5k body → unbounded bundled files, with script code never entering context). The enforcement is what makes it work; an unenforced convention degrades to a 3,000-line memory file.

**7. Access mode as injection containment.** `access: "read_only"` on a mounted store, enforced at the filesystem level. Anthropic's warning is the clearest statement of the threat anyone publishes: a successful injection writes to the store, and "later sessions then read that content as trusted memory" — a persistent, cross-session compromise. The mitigation is architectural, not a classifier: split reference material (read-only, many sessions) from agent scratch (read-write, narrow scope). Google names the same threat as "memory poisoning" and recommends Model Armor on both directions; Microsoft recommends Content Safety on data entering *and leaving* memory.

**8. Dry-run deletion.** Google `:purge{filter, force}` where `force: false` validates without executing. For a predicate-based erasure cascade this is the difference between a confident GDPR workflow and one nobody dares run. Pair it with TTL granularity by write-cause (Google's `granularTtlConfig`: separate `createTtl`, `generateCreatedTtl`, `generateUpdatedTtl` — app-authored facts and LLM-inferred facts should not expire on the same clock).

**Two anti-patterns to avoid, both shipped by major vendors this year.** `DELETE /v1/conversations/{id}` on OpenAI: "Items in the conversation will not be deleted" — a container delete that orphans its children is an erasure-cascade trap. And AWS AgentCore's `eventExpiryDuration` covers raw events only; extracted long-term records have no documented auto-expiry and there is **no per-actor purge call**, so "delete everything about this user" means enumerating namespaces yourself. Both are cautionary tales for anyone designing a facts/sources model with a cascade: derived records need their own lifecycle, and the delete API needs to know the derivation graph.

## 2. Per-provider detail

### 2.1 Anthropic

**Memory tool** — GA (beta 2025-09-29 → GA 2026-02-17). Entire config: `{"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"}`. Client-executes six commands: `view` (`path`, optional `view_range: [start, end]`, `-1` = to EOF), `create` (`file_text`), `str_replace` (`old_str`, optional `new_str` — omit to delete), `insert` (`insert_line`, `insert_text`; 0 = prepend), `delete`, `rename` (`old_path`, `new_path`). The API auto-injects into the system prompt:

> `IMPORTANT: ALWAYS VIEW YOUR MEMORY DIRECTORY BEFORE DOING ANYTHING ELSE. … ASSUME INTERRUPTION: Your context window might be reset at any moment, so you risk losing any progress that is not recorded in your memory directory.`

Published results (2025-09-29): memory tool + context editing = **+39% over baseline** on an agentic-search eval; context editing alone **+29%**; **84% token reduction** on a 100-turn web-search eval that otherwise failed on context exhaustion.

**Memory stores** — beta, `agent-memory-2026-07-22`.

```
POST   /v1/memory_stores                              {name, description}
GET|POST|DELETE /v1/memory_stores/{id}                + /archive (one-way)
POST   /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memories                {path, content}
GET    /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memories?path_prefix=/&depth=0|1
GET|POST|DELETE /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memories/{mem_id}
GET    /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memory_versions?memory_id=...
GET    /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memory_versions/{ver_id}
POST   /v1/memory_stores/{id}/memory_versions/{ver_id}/redact
```

Attach at session creation only (not hot-attachable):

```json
{"resources": [{"type": "memory_store", "memory_store_id": "memstore_01…",
  "access": "read_write", "instructions": "Check before starting any task."}]}
```

Mount slug is display-name lowercased with non-alphanumeric runs → single hyphen; **read `mount_path` from the resource rather than constructing it**. Writes elsewhere under `/mnt/memory/` land in container-local scratch and are lost. Optimistic concurrency:

```json
{"content": "CORRECTED: …", "precondition": {"type": "content_sha256", "content_sha256": "<sha>"}}
```

A version that is the current head **cannot** be redacted — write a new version first. Webhooks exist for `memory_store.created|archived|deleted` (note: `created` also fires when "an Anthropic-operated process… clones one of your existing stores" — i.e. a dream). Individual memories emit no events.

**Dreams** — `POST /v1/dreams` with `inputs: [{type: "memory_store", …}, {type: "sessions", session_ids: [...]}]`, `model`, `instructions`. Status `pending → running → completed|failed|canceled`; `session_id` points at the underlying session so you can stream the pipeline. Key property: **the input store is never modified** — output is a new store you review and adopt or discard. Doc is explicit that instructions steer *synthesis*, not line edits: "imperative directives that target specific lines … generally produce no change."

**Context editing** — `context_management.edits[]`. `clear_tool_uses_20250919`: `trigger` (default `{input_tokens, 100000}`), `keep` (default `{tool_uses, 3}`), `clear_at_least`, `exclude_tools`, `clear_tool_inputs`. `clear_thinking_20251015`: `keep: "all" | {thinking_turns, N}` (Opus 4.5+/Sonnet 4.6+ default to keeping all). **`clear_thinking` must be listed first.** Client keeps the full history; edits are server-side.

**Compaction** — `{"type": "compact_20260112", "trigger": {"input_tokens", 150000}, "pause_after_compaction": false, "instructions": null}`. Min trigger 50,000. `instructions` **fully replaces** the default prompt. Emits a `compaction` content block; everything before it is dropped on subsequent requests. Bill correctly by summing `usage.iterations[]` — the top-level counters exclude the compaction pass. Re-sending an existing compaction block costs nothing extra.

**Skills** — three-level progressive disclosure: metadata (~100 tok/skill, always), SKILL.md body (<5k tok, on trigger), bundled files (0 until read; scripts run via bash so **their code never enters context**). `container: {skills: [{type: "anthropic"|"custom", skill_id, version}]}`.

**Tool search** — GA. `defer_loading: true` per tool (max 10,000 deferred; ≥1 must stay loaded). Vendor numbers: **85% token reduction** (77k → 8.7k), Opus 4.5 MCP accuracy **79.5% → 88.1%**, Opus 4 **49% → 74%**. Deferred tools are stripped from the cache prefix, so **`defer_loading` preserves prompt caching**; discovered tools expand inline in the body. Programmatic tool calling: 43,588 → 27,297 tokens (**−37%**).

**Prompt caching economics** — 5m write **1.25x**, 1h write **2x**, read **0.1x**. Min cacheable: Opus 5 / Fable 5 / Mythos 5 **512**; Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / 4.6 / 4.5 / Opus 4.1 **1,024**; Opus 4.7 **2,048**; Opus 4.6 / 4.5 / Haiku 4.5 **4,096**. Max 4 breakpoints; 20-block lookback. Hierarchy `tools → system → messages`.

**Claude Code** — CLAUDE.md hierarchy (managed policy → `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` → `./CLAUDE.md` → `./CLAUDE.local.md`), `@path` imports (depth 4, external imports require approval), `.claude/rules/*.md` with `paths:` frontmatter for path-scoped loading. **Auto memory** (`autoMemoryEnabled`, on by default): `MEMORY.md` index capped at **200 lines / 25 KB**, topic files loaded on demand, `modified` ISO timestamp frontmatter written on each save. The harness *enforces* the cap: near the limit it reminds Claude to shorten; over it, the write succeeds but returns an error telling Claude to rewrite the index. **What survives compaction**: project-root CLAUDE.md and auto memory are **re-injected from disk**; path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md are lost until re-triggered; skill bodies re-inject capped at 5,000 tok/skill and 25,000 total, oldest dropped.

**Compliance** (feature eligibility table): memory tool **ZDR ✓ HIPAA ✓** (client-side); context editing and compaction **ZDR ✓ HIPAA ✗**; Skills and Managed Agents (incl. memory stores) **ZDR ✗ HIPAA ✗** — "Sessions are stateful resources; transcripts persist until you delete them."

### 2.2 OpenAI

No memory service. The durable-state answer is **Conversations** (indefinite retention, exempt from the 30-day response TTL) plus **Vector Stores** for retrieval. The actual *memory* work — extraction, consolidation, forgetting — only exists in the **beta Agents SDK sandbox**, and it is file-based:

```
memories/
├── memory_summary.md            # auto-injected into the developer prompt at run start
├── MEMORY.md                    # keyword index the agent greps
├── raw_memories/<rollout-id>.md
└── rollout_summaries/<rollout-id>_<slug>.md
sessions/<rollout-id>.jsonl
```

Two-phase generation: (1) a memory model summarizes the accumulated conversation; (2) a consolidation agent rewrites `MEMORY.md` + `memory_summary.md`. `Memory(generate=None)` = read-only, `Memory(read=None)` = generate-only. Scoping is by `MemoryLayoutConfig`, **not by agent name** — same layout + same memory conversation ID means shared memory. Conversation ID priority: explicit `conversation_id` → `session.session_id` → `RunConfig.group_id` → per-run auto ID.

Codex CLI uses the *same* two-file pattern, which is the clearest signal of OpenAI's converging house style. `AGENTS.md` remains static, manually maintained, with a reported 32 KiB silent-truncation ceiling (secondary source).

Session protocol (four methods): `get_items(limit)`, `add_items(items)`, `pop_item()`, `clear_session()`. Backends now include `SQLiteSession`, `AsyncSQLiteSession`, `RedisSession`, `SQLAlchemySession`, `MongoDBSession`, `DaprSession`, `AdvancedSQLiteSession` (branching), `EncryptedSession` (wrapper, TTL), `OpenAIConversationsSession`, `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession`.

`/v1/skills` (create/version/set-default, `files[]` maxItems 500) is **the only OpenAI context primitive with real versioning**, and it's in the spec with no narrative guide.

AgentKit's Agent Builder + Evals + reusable Prompts wind down **2026-11-30** (read-only 2026-10-31); ChatKit survives.

### 2.3 Google

Memory Bank is the most complete managed memory service shipped by anyone. Three interchangeable parents: `reasoningEngines/{re}`, the new top-level `memoryBanks/{mb}`, or shorthand.

```
POST .../memories:generate      # vertexSessionSource | directContentsSource | directMemoriesSource (≤5)
POST .../memories:retrieve      # scope + similaritySearchParams{searchQuery, topK} | simpleRetrievalParams
POST .../memories:ingestEvents  # GA 2026-07-08; streamId + generationTriggerConfig
POST .../memories:purge         # filter (AIP-160) + force (dry-run when false)
POST .../memories/{m}:rollback  # targetRevisionId
GET  .../memories/{m}/revisions[/{rev}]
POST .../memories:retrieveProfiles   # v1beta1 only
```

GA/preview split determined by diffing `v1` vs `v1beta1` discovery docs: everything is in `v1` **except** `retrieveProfiles` and the structured-profile schemas — so profiles are GA-*announced* (2026-07-15) but v1beta1-*served*.

`scope` is one concept doing three jobs, all exact-set-equality (order-insensitive, **case-sensitive**): isolation boundary, consolidation candidate set, and retrieval predicate. From a session source it defaults to `{"user_id": session.user_id}`.

Bank config (`ReasoningEngineContextSpec.memoryBankConfig`): `generationConfig.model` (default `gemini-3.5-flash`), `similaritySearchConfig.embeddingModel` (default `text-embedding-005`; `gemini-embedding-2` only on `global`/`us`/`eu`), `ttlConfig`, `customizationConfigs[]` with `scopeKeys[]` (most-specific-wins, one empty-keys default), `memoryTopics[]`, `generateMemoriesExamples[]`, `consolidationConfig.revisionsPerCandidateCount`, `enableThirdPersonMemories`.

Topics: managed enum `USER_PERSONAL_INFO`, `USER_PREFERENCES`, `KEY_CONVERSATION_DETAILS`, `EXPLICIT_INSTRUCTIONS`; custom via `CustomMemoryTopic{label, description}`, selectable per request via `allowedTopics[]`.

ADK: `BaseMemoryService` now has `add_session_to_memory`, `add_events_to_memory` (delta writes mid-session), `add_memory`, `search_memory`. `preload_memory` = auto-injected at turn start; `load_memory` = model-decided. Note `add_memory` defaults to `memories.create`; pass `custom_metadata={"enable_consolidation": True}` to route through `memories.generate` instead. State prefixes: none = session, `user:` = cross-session per user, `app:` = global, `temp:` = discarded after the invocation.

RAG Engine has a first-class `RagCorpus.corpusTypeConfig.memoryCorpus{llmParser}` — this is the substrate behind `VertexAiRagMemoryService`, and it's raw-transcript vector retrieval, explicitly positioned as the alternative when you want transcripts rather than LLM-extracted facts.

### 2.4 Microsoft & AWS

**Foundry Memory** (preview, `api-version=2025-11-15-preview`) — note you'll run **two api-versions in one app**, since agents use `v1`. Store options: `chat_summary_enabled`, `user_profile_enabled`, `procedural_memory_enabled`, `default_ttl_seconds` (0 = never), and `user_profile_details`, a natural-language steering string used both to prioritize and to exclude ("Avoid irrelevant or sensitive data, such as age, financials, precise location, and credentials"). Tool: `{"type": "memory_search_preview", "memory_store_name", "scope", "update_delay"}` — `update_delay` is seconds of inactivity before extraction, **default 300**. Recommended read pattern: `search_memories` **without** `items` → static profile memories injected at conversation start; **with** `items` → contextual memories per turn.

**AgentCore Memory** — control plane (`bedrock-agentcore-control`) vs data plane (`bedrock-agentcore`) are separate services. Five strategies as a union: `semanticMemoryStrategy`, `summaryMemoryStrategy`, `userPreferenceMemoryStrategy`, `episodicMemoryStrategy`, `customMemoryStrategy`. Steps are extraction / consolidation / **reflection** (episodic only). Prompt override field is **`appendToPrompt`** and the doc warns it *replaces* the default instructions — the name lies. You may not rename the consolidation operations `AddMemory`/`UpdateMemory` or the pipeline fails.

Escape hatches worth knowing: `extractionMode: "SKIP"` on `CreateEvent` stores raw but excludes from extraction; `selfManagedConfiguration` gives you `triggerConditions` (`messageBasedTrigger.messageCount`, `tokenBasedTrigger.tokenCount`, `timeBasedTrigger.idleSessionTimeout`) → SNS → S3 payload → your pipeline → `BatchCreateMemoryRecords`.

Metadata pre-filtering (Apr 2026): `indexedKeys` (`STRING`/`STRINGLIST`/`NUMBER`, **cannot be removed, no backfill**), 9 operators, max 5 filters, AND only. `extractionType: STRICTLY_CONSISTENT` copies a value verbatim and **partitions extraction/consolidation** so records from different value groups never merge.

Namespace hygiene: AWS explicitly says use a **trailing slash** (`/actors/Alice/` not `/actors/Alice`) to avoid prefix collisions in multi-tenant apps.

---

## 3. Cross-cutting patterns

**Context rot is now measured, not folklore.** Chroma's study (2025-07-14, 18 models, needle-in-haystack variants + LongMemEval at ~113k tokens + repeated-words) found degradation "in surprising and non-uniform ways," that "even a single distractor reduces performance," and — counterintuitively — that **shuffling the haystack and destroying local coherence *improves* performance**. Anthropic's framing: context is a finite "attention budget," and the goal is "the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome."

**The three-way tradeoff is now a four-way one, and every provider picks differently.**

| Approach | Cost | Failure mode | Who does it server-side |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prune** (drop tool results/thinking) | Cheap, invalidates cache from the cut point | Silent loss of detail | Anthropic `clear_tool_uses_*` |
| **Compact** (summarize prefix) | Extra sampling pass, billed | Lossy; irreversible | Anthropic `compact_20260112`; OpenAI `context_management` + `/responses/compact` |
| **Externalize** (write to memory) | Storage + retrieval latency | Staleness, contradiction, poisoning | Anthropic stores, Google Memory Bank, AWS AgentCore, MS Foundry |
| **Defer** (don't load until asked) | Near-free, cache-preserving | Discovery misses | Anthropic tool search + Skills; OpenAI/Codex `MEMORY.md` grep |

Deferral is the underrated one. It's the only strategy with no accuracy tax, and Anthropic's tool-search numbers (85% fewer definition tokens *and* accuracy 79.5% → 88.1%) show pruning the menu improves choice.

**Compaction is not always better than a hard reset.** Anthropic's own harness team: "Context resets worked better than compaction for preventing model 'context anxiety'" — they used clean-slate sessions with a handoff artifact instead. Measured on one build: solo agent 20 min / $9 producing non-functional output vs full harness 6 hr / $200 producing a working app.

**Structured note-taking is the convergent house style.** Independently, four vendors landed on *a size-capped index file plus on-demand detail files*: Anthropic Claude Code (`MEMORY.md`, 200 lines/25 KB, harness errors if exceeded), OpenAI Agents SDK sandbox and Codex CLI (`memory_summary.md` injected + `MEMORY.md` grepped), Anthropic Skills (metadata → body → bundled files), and Anthropic's long-running agent harness (`claude-progress.txt` + `feature_list.json` + `init.sh` + git). The scientific-computing writeup calls `CHANGELOG.md` "the agent's portable long-term memory, acting as a sort of lab notes" and stresses recording **failed approaches and why they didn't work** — negative results are the highest-value memory and the least likely to be re-derived.

**Sub-agent isolation is a memory strategy with a known price.** Anthropic: agents use ~4x the tokens of chat; multi-agent ~**15x**. Orchestrator-worker with Opus 4 lead + Sonnet 4 subagents beat single-agent Opus 4 by **90.2%**; token usage alone explained **80% of variance** on BrowseComp. Subagents return 1,000–2,000-token summaries rather than raw context. In Claude Code, a subagent inherits CLAUDE.md but **not** the parent's auto memory — it gets its own directory via `memory: user|project|local`.

**Code execution as a context filter.** Anthropic's MCP-via-code post reports **150,000 → 2,000 tokens (98.7%)** by presenting servers as a `./servers/<server>/<tool>.ts` filesystem the model navigates, and notes the privacy consequence: "intermediate results stay in the execution environment by default," so PII can move between tools without entering model context.

**Interop does not exist.** MCP has five primitives (tools, resources, prompts, sampling, roots/elicitation) and **no memory primitive**. There is a W3C **AI Agent Memory Interoperability Community Group** (launched 2026-06-03, charter 2026-06-19, 17 participants) referencing IETF draft **`draft-saihm-memory-protocol`** — but be clear-eyed: the group's chair and the draft's sole author are the same person, the draft is an Independent Submission (not IETF-endorsed, expires 2026-11-28), it's blockchain-flavored (ML-DSA-65 signatures, public-chain anchoring, wallet-derived keys), and **no deliverables have been published**. No vendor backing. Treat as noise, not signal.

---

## 4. What's actually novel — the 8 worth stealing

**1. Immutable version-per-mutation that outlives its parent, plus redact-in-place.** Anthropic memory versions (`memver_...`) belong to the *store*, not the memory, carry a `created_by` actor, and survive deletion of the memory. `/redact` scrubs content while preserving who-did-what-when. Google goes further: revisions carry `extractedMemories[].context` = "the explanation of why the information was extracted from the source content" — the pre-consolidation evidence *and the rationale*. Contrast ChatGPT Dreaming, which has better consolidation and essentially no audit trail. **If you build one thing from this list, build this.** Redact-not-delete is the correct GDPR primitive for derived facts.

**2. `content_sha256` optimistic concurrency on memory writes.** Two agents editing the same memory is not hypothetical once you have background consolidation. Anthropic's `precondition: {type: "content_sha256", content_sha256}` is a two-field solution that turns a lost-update bug into a retry. Nobody else ships this.

**3. Consolidation as an offline job that writes to a *new* store and never mutates the input.** Anthropic dreams: input store untouched, output store reviewable, discard if bad. This makes the scariest operation in a memory system (an LLM rewriting your facts) safe to run, and makes it A/B-testable. AWS and Google both consolidate in place; Google mitigates with rollback, AWS doesn't mitigate at all.

**4. `scope` as one exact-match KV dict doing three jobs.** Google's `scope` is simultaneously the isolation boundary, the consolidation candidate set, and the retrieval predicate — with exact set equality, immutable after creation, and IAM Conditions enforceable per scope. One concept, three guarantees, no drift between them. Compare AWS, where namespaces do the *who* and metadata does the *what* — and AWS has to explicitly warn you not to use metadata for tenant isolation because it's "a security-through-convention model that breaks on any missed filter."

**5. A consolidation *partition key*.** AWS `extractionType: STRICTLY_CONSISTENT` (value copied verbatim, LLM never consulted, and records from different value groups never merge) and Google `metadataMergeStrategy: REQUIRE_EXACT_MATCH` solve the same problem: guaranteeing the merge step cannot cross a boundary you care about. If you have any multi-tenant, per-client, or per-legal-entity dimension, you need this or the LLM will eventually blend two clients' facts into one.

**6. Progressive disclosure with a machine-enforced index cap.** Not just "have an index file" — Claude Code *measures* `MEMORY.md` after each write against 200 lines / 25 KB, reminds Claude when near, and **returns an error** when over, because content past the limit is silently dropped on next load. Skills do the same shape at a different scale (~100 tok metadata → <5k body → unbounded bundled files, with script code never entering context). The enforcement is what makes it work; an unenforced convention degrades to a 3,000-line memory file.

**7. Access mode as injection containment.** `access: "read_only"` on a mounted store, enforced at the filesystem level. Anthropic's warning is the clearest statement of the threat anyone publishes: a successful injection writes to the store, and "later sessions then read that content as trusted memory" — a persistent, cross-session compromise. The mitigation is architectural, not a classifier: split reference material (read-only, many sessions) from agent scratch (read-write, narrow scope). Google names the same threat as "memory poisoning" and recommends Model Armor on both directions; Microsoft recommends Content Safety on data entering *and leaving* memory.

**8. Dry-run deletion.** Google `:purge{filter, force}` where `force: false` validates without executing. For a predicate-based erasure cascade this is the difference between a confident GDPR workflow and one nobody dares run. Pair it with TTL granularity by write-cause (Google's `granularTtlConfig`: separate `createTtl`, `generateCreatedTtl`, `generateUpdatedTtl` — app-authored facts and LLM-inferred facts should not expire on the same clock).

**Two anti-patterns to avoid, both shipped by major vendors this year.** `DELETE /v1/conversations/{id}` on OpenAI: "Items in the conversation will not be deleted" — a container delete that orphans its children is an erasure-cascade trap. And AWS AgentCore's `eventExpiryDuration` covers raw events only; extracted long-term records have no documented auto-expiry and there is **no per-actor purge call**, so "delete everything about this user" means enumerating namespaces yourself. Both are cautionary tales for anyone designing a facts/sources model with a cascade: derived records need their own lifecycle, and the delete API needs to know the derivation graph.

## 1. HippoRAG 2 (arXiv:2502.14802) — what actually changed vs v1

Source: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2502.14802 · https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14802

### Framing `[V]`
The paper posits three properties of human long-term memory a RAG system must approximate, and maps each to a benchmark family:

| Aspect | Definition (paper's words) | Benchmarks |
|---|---|---|
| **Factual memory** | "ability to recall and retrieve factual knowledge accurately" | NaturalQuestions, PopQA (*simple QA*) |
| **Sense-making** | "ability to interpret larger, more complex, or uncertain contexts" | NarrativeQA (*discourse understanding*) |
| **Associativity** | "capacity to draw multi-hop connections between disparate pieces of knowledge" | MuSiQue, 2Wiki, HotpotQA, LV-Eval |

Note: there is **no separate custom "sense-making" benchmark** — it's NarrativeQA under the "discourse understanding" heading. `[V]`

Brain mapping `[V]`: LLM = artificial neocortex; embedding encoder = parahippocampal region (PHR, detects synonymy); the KG = artificial hippocampus/hippocampal index.

### The motivating failure of HippoRAG 1 `[V]`
Two distinct problems drove the redesign:
1. **Context loss.** Entity-only (phrase) nodes discard the passage context, so the graph can't support contextual/discourse reasoning.
2. **Simple-QA regression.** HippoRAG 1 (and all structure-augmented RAG methods) *underperformed plain dense retrieval on factual QA*. Concretely, HippoRAG 1 got **44.4 passage recall@5 on NQ vs NV-Embed-v2's 75.4** — a catastrophic regression the redesign had to fix. This is the single most important lesson for your project: **a graph layer that helps multi-hop can badly hurt the simple lookup case unless dense retrieval is fused back in.**

### The five changes

**(a) Passage nodes reintroduced into the graph** `[V]`
v1's graph had phrase nodes only. v2 adds every corpus passage as a node. Three edge types:
- **Relation edges** — phrase↔phrase, from OpenIE triples (subject–object).
- **Synonym edges** — phrase↔phrase, when embedding cosine similarity exceeds a threshold; **threshold = 0.8**.
- **Context edges** — passage→phrase, labeled `"contains"`: "each passage in the corpus is treated as a passage node, with the context edge labeled 'contains' connecting the passage to all phrases derived from this passage."

**(b) Query-to-triple linking (replaces NER-to-node)** `[V]`
v1 ran NER on the query, then matched extracted entities to phrase nodes. v2 embeds the **entire query text** and scores it against **embeddings of whole triples** (the serialized subject-relation-object string). The paper explicitly compares all three variants; query-to-triple wins decisively. Rationale: it "provides a more comprehensive understanding of the query's intent."

**(c) "Recognition memory" — the LLM triple filter** `[V]`
Named after the neuroscience distinction between *active recall* and *identification with external cues*. Mechanism:
1. Embedding retrieval returns **top-5 triples** ranked by the retriever.
2. An LLM (**Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct**, also tested with GPT-4o-mini) filters them → `T′ ⊆ T`.
3. **Temperature = 0.0.**
4. The prompt was **tuned with the DSPy MIPROv2 optimizer** using Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct — instructions *and* few-shot demonstrations were optimized, not hand-written. Full prompt is in Appendix A.

**(d) Deeper contextualization** `[V]` — passage node embeddings feed the PPR seeding directly, so activation isn't purely phrase-mediated.

**(e) The PPR reset-probability distribution — the implementable core** `[V]`

This is the part you want for your fact graph:
- **Phrase seed nodes:** at most **5**, drawn from the filtered triples. Each phrase node's score = **the average score of all filtered triples in which it appears**. Reset probability = that score, directly.
- **Passage seed nodes:** **all** passage nodes are seeds. Reset probability ∝ **embedding similarity to the query**.
- **Balancing:** "passage node scores are multiplied by a weight factor to balance the influence of phrase nodes and passage nodes." Tuned optimum: **weight factor = 0.05**.
- **PPR damping factor = 0.5.**
- Final: passages ranked by resulting PageRank score; top-k passed to the reader.

The 0.05 weight is worth internalizing: **phrase-node activation dominates by ~20x**; the passage seeds act as a dense-retrieval prior that prevents the simple-QA collapse rather than driving the ranking.

## 2. MemGPT (arXiv:2310.08560) — mechanism

Source: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2310.08560

### Memory hierarchy `[V]`
**Main context** (= the prompt) has three contiguous sections:
1. **System instructions** — read-only, static; contains the control-flow directives and function-usage documentation.
2. **Working context** — fixed-size, read/write unstructured text block, **writable only via function calls**; holds "key facts, preferences, and other important information about the user."
3. **FIFO queue** — rolling message history (user/agent messages, system alerts, function I/O). **Index 0 of the queue is a system message holding the recursive summary of everything evicted so far.**

**External context**: **archival storage** (read/write DB for arbitrary-length text objects) and **recall storage** (the full message DB — every message ever, verbatim).

The paper assigns **no fixed token budget percentages** to the three main-context sections. `[V]`

### Function-calling memory `[V]`
- Memory edits and retrieval are **entirely self-directed**: "MemGPT autonomously updates and searches through its own memory based on the current context."
- Flow: LLM emits a string → MemGPT **parser validates** → function executor runs it → result **including runtime errors** is fed back into main context.
- Error feedback is deliberate: "Runtime errors that occur (e.g. trying to add to main context when it is already at maximum capacity), are then fed back to the processor by MemGPT. This feedback loop enables the system to learn from its actions and adjust its behavior accordingly."
- Retrieval functions implement **pagination** so a result set cannot overflow the window.
- The paper does **not** publish an exhaustive function-name list. `[V]`

### Heartbeat / yield-control `[V]`
- Functions take a special argument **`request_heartbeat=true`**. When set, "MemGPT will add the function output to main context and … run the LLM processor immediately."
- Absence of the flag is a **yield**: "MemGPT will not run the LLM processor until the next external event trigger (e.g. a user message or scheduled interrupt)."
- This enables **function chaining** — multiple sequential calls before returning control to the user, e.g. paging through results or collating across documents.
- **Events** are the generalized input: user messages, system messages (capacity warnings), user interactions, and **timed events on a schedule**. That last one is exactly the hook for a nightly consolidation job.

### Queue manager `[V]`
Six responsibilities: (1) append incoming messages to the FIFO queue; (2) concatenate prompt tokens and trigger inference; (3) write incoming messages and LLM outputs to **recall storage**; (4) append retrieved messages back into the queue; (5) control context overflow via eviction policy; (6) perform recursive summarization on eviction.

### Thresholds — the exact numbers `[V]`
- **Warning token count ≈ 70% of the context window** → queue manager inserts a system message warning of impending eviction (the "**memory pressure**" warning). This exists so the LLM can proactively flush important facts from the FIFO queue into working context or archival storage *before* they're lost.
- **Flush token count ≈ 100% of the context window** → eviction fires.
- **On flush, evict ~50% of the context window** worth of messages, and generate a **new recursive summary from (existing recursive summary + newly evicted messages)**.
- Evicted messages remain **indefinitely in recall storage** and are re-readable via function call.
- The paper presents these as example values ("e.g."), not hard constants. `[V]`

### DMR benchmark `[V]`
- Built from **Multi-Session Chat (MSC)** by adding a **6th session** to MSC's original five (~a dozen messages each).
- Q/A pairs were generated by "a separate LLM that was instructed to write a question … that could only be answered correctly using knowledge gained from the past sessions."
- Exact question count **not stated** in the paper text I retrieved. `[V that it's absent]` — commonly cited as **500 questions** `[R, unverified]`.
- Metrics: **ROUGE-L recall** (chosen to be robust to response verbosity) **plus an LLM judge** "instructed to evaluate whether or not the generated response is consistent with the gold response."

| Model | Accuracy | ROUGE-L |
|---|---|---|
| GPT-3.5 Turbo | 38.7% | 0.394 |
| **MemGPT (GPT-3.5)** | **66.9%** | **0.629** |
| GPT-4 | 32.1% | 0.296 |
| **MemGPT (GPT-4)** | **92.5%** | **0.814** |
| GPT-4 Turbo | 35.3% | 0.359 |
| **MemGPT (GPT-4 Turbo)** | **93.4%** | **0.827** |

### Why DMR saturated — the known weaknesses
- **Structurally trivial.** Each question is answerable from a *single* prior session turn. It's single-hop needle retrieval, not memory management. `[V from design]`
- **93.4% at publication** left ~6 points of headroom, most of it judge noise. Modern systems cluster at 95%+, so it no longer discriminates. `[R]`
- **The baselines are pathological.** Note GPT-4 (32.1%) scores *worse* than GPT-3.5 (38.7%) — this is a prompting/verbosity artifact of the fixed-context baseline, not a capability signal. Any benchmark where the stronger model loses to the weaker one on the baseline arm is measuring format compliance as much as memory. `[V numbers; R interpretation]`
- **ROUGE-L on short factoid answers is near-degenerate** — it rewards lexical echo of the gold string. `[R]`
- **It tests recall only, never forgetting or contradiction.** No superseded facts, no deletions, no conflicting updates. This is precisely the gap the 2026 ForgetEval work (§6) was built to fill, and it's the gap that matters most for your system.

Other MemGPT results `[V]`: conversation-opener CSIM — human 0.800/0.800/1.000 (SIM-1/SIM-3/SIM-H), GPT-4 Turbo 0.857/0.828/0.767, MemGPT exceeds human baseline. Multi-doc QA: 50 questions from NaturalQuestions-Open (late-2018 Wikipedia); MemGPT stays flat as document count grows while baselines plateau at retriever ceiling. Nested key-value retrieval: 140 UUID pairs (~8k tokens), nesting 0–4; **GPT-4 hits 0% by 3 nesting levels; MemGPT is unaffected by nesting depth.**

## 3. Reflexion (arXiv:2303.11366)

Source: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2303.11366

### The triad `[V]`
- **Actor `M_a`** — LLM prompted to generate text and actions conditioned on state observations. Instantiated as Chain-of-Thought or ReAct.
- **Evaluator `M_e`** — scores the trajectory. Three modes by task type: **exact-match grading** (reasoning), **pre-defined heuristics or an LLM binary classifier** (decision-making), **test execution results** (programming).
- **Self-Reflection `M_sr`** — an LLM that turns a sparse reward + the trajectory into verbal feedback. "plays a crucial role … by generating verbal self-reflections to provide valuable feedback for future trials."

Models used across experiments: GPT-3, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, text-davinci-003. `[V]`

### Verbal reinforcement `[V]`
"Reflexion converts binary or scalar feedback from the environment into verbal feedback in the form of a textual summary, which is then added as additional context for the LLM agent in the next episode." No gradient updates — the "policy" is the prompt.

### The memory buffer and its window — the number you asked about `[V]`
> "In practice, we bound mem by a maximum number of stored experiences, **Ω (usually set to 1-3)** to adhere to max context LLM limitations."

Your recollection of 1–3 is correct and verbatim. The reflections are stored as `sr_t` and appended after each trial; the window slides.

**Short-term vs long-term** `[V]`: short-term = the current trajectory (fine-grained recent detail); long-term = the Self-Reflection outputs in the buffer. "At inference time, the Actor conditions its decisions on short and long-term memory, similar to the way that humans remember fine-grain recent details while also recalling distilled important experiences from long-term memory."

**Algorithm 1** `[V]`: init Actor/Evaluator/Self-Reflection → generate τ₀ → evaluate → generate sr₀ → loop {generate τ_t, evaluate, generate sr_t, append to mem, t++} until success or max trials.

### Results `[V]`
- **HumanEval (Python) pass@1: 91%**, vs prior SOTA GPT-4 at 80%. Your recollection is confirmed.
- **MBPP (Python): 77.1% Reflexion vs 80.1% GPT-4** — Reflexion is **worse**. Worth knowing: self-reflection is not universally positive; on MBPP the reflection loop hurt.
- HumanEval (Rust): 68.0% vs 60.0%. MBPP (Rust): 75.4% vs 70.9%. LeetcodeHard (Python): 15.0% vs 7.5%.
- **HotpotQA: +20% absolute** over baselines across 100 questions.
- **ALFWorld: 130/134 tasks completed; +22% absolute over strong baselines in 12 iterative learning steps.**

## 4. Voyager (arXiv:2305.16291) — the skill library as procedural memory

Source: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2305.16291

### Indexing and retrieval — the concrete details `[V]`
- **Storage:** executable **JavaScript** programs (Mineflayer API calls) in a vector DB.
- **Key = the embedding of the skill's *description***, not the code. The description is **LLM-generated** (via GPT-3.5) as a docstring-style summary of what the program does; embedded with **`text-embedding-ada-002`**.
- **Value = the executable program itself.**
- **Retrieval query:** GPT-3.5 generates a **general task suggestion** from agent state + exploration progress; that suggestion (combined with environment feedback) is the retrieval context. Note the asymmetry — you embed a *description of the skill* and query with a *description of the intended task*; both sides are in "intent space," never in code space.
- **Top-k retrieved = 5.** ("top-5 relevant skills," Fig. 4.)
- Retrieved skills go into the code-generation prompt for in-context learning.

### Composition `[V]`
Skills call other skills directly: "Complex skills can be synthesized by composing simpler programs, which compounds Voyager's capabilities rapidly." Enforced by prompt instruction: *"Your function will be reused for building more complex functions. Therefore, you should make it generic and reusable."* Examples: `craftStoneShovel()`, `combatZombieWithSword()`.

### Iterative prompting `[V]`
Three feedback channels into the next code-gen round:
1. **Environment feedback** — intermediate execution state, e.g. *"I cannot make an iron chestplate because I need: 7 more iron ingots"*.
2. **Execution errors** — syntax / invalid-operation errors from the interpreter.
3. **Self-verification** — a **separate GPT-4 agent acting as critic** that checks task success *and* provides constructive critique. Described as strictly more comprehensive than self-reflection because it both verifies and reflects.

**Round limit: "try at most 4 rounds before moving on to the next task."** After 4 failed iterations, the agent asks the curriculum for a different task. Only successful programs are added to the library. `[V]`

### Automatic curriculum `[V]`
- **Temperature 0.1** for the curriculum (vs **0** everywhere else) to encourage task diversity.
- Prompt contains directives, agent state, completed/failed task lists, and **"self-ask questions"** answered by GPT-3.5 with optional wiki lookups.
- Task constraints: must be specific (*"Mine [quantity] [block]"*), achievable given current resources, novel, and **must avoid building/placement tasks requiring visual verification**.
- Warm-up schedule (Table A.1) progressively reveals state: task 0 → core inventory/equipment/nearby blocks/position; task 5 → nearby entities; task 7 → full inventory; task 10 → other blocks + biome; task 15 → health, hunger, time.

**Hyperparameter summary** `[V]`: max exploration prompting iterations **160**; max iterations for zero-shot generalization tasks **50**; code-gen rounds per task **4**; skill retrieval **top-5**; temperature 0.1 (curriculum) / 0 (rest).

## 5. Sleep-time compute (arXiv:2504.13171, Letta + UC Berkeley)

Source: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.13171

### Mechanism `[V]`
Standard test-time: `T_B(q, c) → a` — query and context arrive together, budget `B`.
Sleep-time decomposition:
- **Offline:** `S(c) → c′` — the model "thinks" about the raw context while idle, producing an enriched `c′`.
- **Online:** `T_b(q, c′) → a` with **`b << B`**.

Implementation: function-calling API exposing **`rethink_memory()`** and **`finish_rethinking()`**, with **up to 10 calls** during the sleep phase. The framing: "by anticipating what queries users might ask and pre-computing useful quantities, we can significantly reduce the compute requirements at test-time."

### Benchmark construction `[V]`
- **Stateful GSM-Symbolic** — from GSM-Symbolic **P1 (5,000 examples)** and **P2 (2,500)**, "splitting the existing problems in these datasets into a context and a question." (Example: the narrative setup is context; *"How much longer do they have…"* is the question.)
- **Stateful AIME** — **60 problems** from AIME 2024/2025; "split each AIME [problem] into a sequence of 'statements' … all but the last statement as the context, and the final statement as the query," with manual handling of mid-problem questions.
- **Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic** — P1: **12,043 questions over 1,095 contexts** (original + **10,948 synthetically generated** by o3-mini); P2: **5,497 questions over 500 contexts**.

### Results `[V]`
> "sleep-time compute can reduce the amount of test-time compute needed to achieve the same accuracy by **∼5×** on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME and … by scaling sleep-time compute we can further increase accuracy by up to **13% on Stateful GSM-Symbolic** and **18% on Stateful AIME**."

- Sleep-time compute **generally Pareto-dominates pass@k** (Figs. 5–6), across o1, o3-mini, Claude, and R1.
- **Amortization: "By amortizing sleep-time compute across related queries about the same context using Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic, we can decrease the average cost per query by 2.5×."** This assumes **10 queries per context**; the curve improves monotonically with questions-per-context (Fig. 9). Cost model weights **test-time tokens 10× more expensive than sleep-time tokens**, to reflect the latency-optimized inference premium.

### When it helps and when it doesn't `[V]` — the most actionable finding
- **"sleep-time compute is most effective in settings where the query is more predictable from the context."** They *measure* predictability as **log P(question | context) under the Llama2-70B base model**, and show (Fig. 10) the accuracy gap widening monotonically with predictability.
- **Fails when:** "In settings where the queries are challenging to predict or unrelated to the context, sleep-time compute will be less effective."
- **Also fails at high test-time budget:** with a large sequential budget, the test-time-only baseline sometimes wins. Hypothesis given: "standard test-time compute has the content relevant to the specific question, so there is less distracting information in the prompt." Pre-computation is *added distractor mass* when you can afford to think from scratch.
- **SWE-Features case study:** only ~**1.5×** token reduction at low budgets, and standard test-time compute wins at high budgets (higher precision despite lower recall).

## 6. 2026 work you'd otherwise miss

### 6a. Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting — **the most directly applicable paper in this list**

**arXiv:2606.15903** — *"Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting: An Architectural Study of Agent Memory Across Thirteen System Configurations"*, Dongxu Yang (DeepLethe). Submitted **14 June 2026**, revised 16 June 2026. **Confirmed real.** ForgetEval + all adapters released under **MIT**.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15903 · https://arxiv.org/html/2606.15903

**The thesis** `[V]`: "Where an LLM sits in an agent memory pipeline — between the recall plane that retrieves stored facts and the control plane that mutates them — shapes which forgetting failure modes the system recovers." And the framing observation: **production failures are predominantly *forgetting* failures, not recall failures, yet every existing benchmark measures recall.**

**The Adapter Protocol — the six-method contract** `[V]`:
```python
class Adapter(Protocol):
    name: str
    def reset(self) -> None
    def inscribe(self, text: str) -> int | str
    def recall_texts(self, q: str, k: int) -> list[str]
    # optional — NotImplementedError → scored N/A
    def supersede(self, old_q: str, new: str) -> None
    def release(self, q: str) -> int
    def purge(self, q: str) -> int
```
Critically: "The Protocol is a behavioural contract, not a syntactic one. An adapter … can implement `supersede(old_q, new)` as `delete(best_match(old_q)) → add(new)`" and still pass. Three mandatory (reset/inscribe/recall), three optional control-plane ops.

**The thirteen configurations** `[V]`:
1. **Lethe v1** — deterministic baseline, BM25-based purge
2. **LangGraph InMemoryStore** — vector store with soft-delete
3. **Mem0 v2.0.2 (infer=False)** — LLM-routed ADD/UPDATE/DELETE
4. **Mem0 v2.0.2 (infer=True)**
5. **MemPalace** — verbatim-retention reference, *no deletion primitives at all*
6. **Lethe + LLM (DeepSeek-V3)** — mutation-time hook
7. **LangGraph + LLM** — same hook, different backbone
8. **A-MEM** — inscribe-time LLM, Zettelkasten linking
9. **Mem0 + v3 (infer=True)** — inscribe-time LLM routing (LINK-AND-KEEP router)
10. **Letta v0.16.7** — archival memory, soft-delete
11. **Letta + LLM** — joint inscribe + mutation placement
12. **Graphiti** — temporal KG on Neo4j
13. **HippoRAG** — KG + Personalized PageRank
14. **OpenMemory** — synthetic-embedding vector store

*(The paper's own count of "thirteen" and this enumeration of 14 rows differ by one — the two Mem0 infer settings are likely counted as one system. Flagging rather than papering over.)*

**The three placement regimes** `[V]`:

| Regime | Where the LLM sits | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Deterministic (no LLM)** | Nowhere. `supersede`=lexical match, `release`=TTL/soft-delete, `purge`=BM25/vector match | Lexical & temporal ≥95%; **temporal_qualifier 37/37 = 100%** | Canonicalization collapses: **identifier_obfuscation 5%**, **cross_lingual 0%** |
| **2. Inscribe-time LLM** | Inside `inscribe()` — extracts tags, entity links, normalized forms | **Canonicalization 100%** (identifier_obfuscation 100%, cross_lingual 100%) | **Intent-aware deletion 0%** — prefix_collision 0%, compound_fact 0% |
| **3. Mutation-time hook** | Inside supersede/purge/release *planning*, via narrow JSON contract | **Intent-aware deletion 78–85%**; **+22.6 to +24.1 pt overall lift** | **~2.3 s/case** vs 64–191 ms deterministic (**~32× slower**) |

Summary lift: **"deterministic 70.1–70.7% → hook 93.3–94.2%"** (on the 345 non-compound-fact cases).

**ForgetEval** `[V]`:
- **Templated suite: 1,000 cases**, five structural families — **supersession, decay, amnesia, purge, drift**. Deterministic generation, **seed=42**, **4 distractors per case**.
- **Pass condition** (deterministic substring match): `must_contain ⊆ top-10 blob` **AND** `must_not_contain ∩ top-10 blob = ∅`.
- **Adversarial layer: 385 cases = 132 hand-crafted core + 253 LLM-drafted, oracle-validated.**

| Category | N | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| negation_trap | 40 | Negated fact must not be confused with affirmative |
| shared_attribute | 40 | Two entities share an attribute; forget one, preserve the link |
| **compound_fact** | 40 | One sentence, two distinct-topic facts; **partial edit required** |
| prefix_collision | 39 | Two IDs share a long prefix (`alice@x` vs `alice.smith@x`) |
| recursive_supersession | 39 | Chrome→Brave→Chrome; latest state matches an earlier-superseded value |
| paraphrase_supersession | 38 | New fact lexically distant from old |
| identifier_obfuscation | 38 | Same ID, different surface form (case, whitespace, separators) |
| cross_lingual_identifier | 38 | Entity under different scripts (romanized vs source-script) |
| temporal_qualifier | 37 | Date-stamped supersession chains |
| substring_trap | 36 | must-not substring embedded inside a distractor |
| **Total** | **385** | *(sums exactly)* |

Validation `[V]`: **Fleiss' κ = 0.958** (10 annotators, 100-case sample), **99.1% observed agreement** over 1,000 labels; plus a **77-case external-authored subset** from 4 blind contributors.

**Axis-flip result** `[V]` — the paper's sharpest point: **MemPalace scores 0/385 (0%) on ForgetEval-Adv but 60/150 (40%) on the recall-heavy Memora benchmark.** A system with no deletion primitive looks *mid-pack* on every recall benchmark and *catastrophic* on a forgetting benchmark.
