**Cost and latency** `[V]`: ~**$0.17 per 385-case run** (≈ **$0.00044 per mutation call**). Per-case latency: **LangGraph ~64 ms**, **Lethe ~74 ms**, **MemPalace ~191 ms**, **Mem0 ~514 ms** (7× slower, includes cold start), **Lethe+LLM ~2.3 s** (mutations only — **recall latency unchanged**).

**The mutation-time hook contract** `[V]`: three JSON-shaped prompts — **`supersede` (planner)**, **`purge_match`**, **`release_match`**. The supersede prompt uses **four-shot examples**. Full prompt text is in Appendix B (not in the HTML body). Model: **DeepSeek-V3 via SiliconFlow**. Cross-LLM ablation: **Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct yields only +8 pt** with category-specific variance; **Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct fails to parse the prompt contract entirely.**

**Practitioner guidance** `[V]`:
- The three regimes have **complementary, non-redundant coverage**. Inscribe-time fixes canonicalization; mutation-time fixes intent-aware deletion; deterministic handles lexical/temporal for free.
- **Joint placement is necessary but not sufficient**: "Letta+LLM lifts overall evaluable 65.5→76.1% … but trails Lethe+LLM (91.7%) for lack of a partial-edit primitive (compound_fact 0/40)."
- **Best configuration = mutation-time hook on a high-recall backbone** (LangGraph+LLM 94.2% > Lethe+LLM 93.3%).
- **compound_fact is a primitive-existence test, not a forgetting-capability test** — three of the four systems score 0/40 "by primitive absence rather than by forgetting failure." Only Lethe exposes `surrender(mode="edit")`. Hence the paper reports 345-case aggregates separately.
- Offline/air-gapped deployments "have no recourse for those categories beyond their store's edit / canonicalization primitives."

**Threats to validity — read these before trusting the numbers** `[V]`:
- **Circularity:** "253/385 cases are LLM-drafted (DeepSeek-V3) and admitted by a single LLM judge (Qwen-2.5-72B), and the LLM hook is also DeepSeek-V3; the recovered categories overlap with where LLM inductive biases are strongest. We cannot fully rule out residual overlap…"
- **The 63–68% "deterministic band" is provenance-dependent, not a true ceiling:** "On the 77-case external-authored subset the band drops to 28–51% … confirming the band is a provenance-dependent saturation, not a true ceiling." On the hand-crafted core subset: **deterministic ~53%, LLM-hook 96–98.5%**; external validation shows **+27.8 pt on Letta+LLM**.
- **Scorer artifacts:** "A 50-case stratified audit of Lethe's deterministic failures finds **30% are scorer artifacts**, confined to prefix_collision … The canonicalization categories that carry the LLM-placement findings contain zero artifacts."
- **English-heavy:** hand-crafted layer is English; cross_lingual covers 9 script families with thin per-family sampling.

### 6b. 2025/2026 surveys and their taxonomies

**"Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents: Mechanisms, Evaluation, and Emerging Frontiers"** — arXiv:2603.07670, Pengfei Du, submitted **8 March 2026**. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.07670 `[V]`

The single best orientation document. Formalization:
```
a_t     = π_θ(x_t, ℛ(M_t, x_t), g_t)
M_{t+1} = U(M_t, x_t, a_t, o_t, r_t)
```
where ℛ = read, U = update, g_t = active goals, o_t = environment feedback, r_t = reward. Key point: **U is not append** — it "summarizes, deduplicates, scores priority, resolves contradictions, and deletes." M_t is treated as a **belief state in a POMDP**, standing in for the unobservable true state.

**Three-dimensional taxonomy** `[V]`:
- **Temporal scope:** working / episodic / semantic / procedural
- **Representational substrate:** context-resident text / vector-indexed stores / structured stores (SQL, KV, KG) / executable repositories / hybrid
- **Control policy:** heuristic (hard-coded rules) / prompted self-control (agent invokes memory ops as tools) / learned (RL-optimized end-to-end)

**Five mechanism families + exemplars** `[V]`:
| Family | Exemplars cited |
|---|---|
| Context-resident compression | Self-Controlled Memory (Liang 2023), rolling & hierarchical summaries |
| Retrieval-augmented stores | RAG (Lewis 2020), RETRO (Borgeaud 2022), RET-LLM (Sun 2024), Self-RAG (Asai 2024) |
| Reflective self-improvement | Reflexion (Shinn 2023), Generative Agents (Park 2023), ExpeL (Zhao 2024), Think-in-Memory (Liu 2024a) |
| Hierarchical virtual context | MemGPT (Packer 2024), JARVIS-1 (Wang 2024b), Cognitive Architectures (Sumers 2024) |
| Policy-learned management | Agentic Memory/AgeMem (Yu 2026), MemLLM (Modarressi 2024) |

**Benchmark critique** `[V]` — three findings worth quoting to your team:
1. **"Despite context windows stretching to 200k tokens, long-context models consistently underperform purpose-built memory systems on tasks requiring selective retrieval and active management."**
2. **"Only MemoryAgentBench tests selective forgetting explicitly. Yet in any long-running deployment, the inability to discard outdated information gradually poisons retrieval precision."**
3. **MemoryArena (2026)**: models near-perfect on LoCoMo **"plummet to 40–60% in MemoryArena"** on interdependent multi-session agentic tasks. MemoryAgentBench tests four competencies — accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, selective forgetting — and **"no current system masters all four … most fail conspicuously on selective forgetting."**

**Four-layer metric stack** `[V]` — directly adoptable as your eval spec:
- L1 **task effectiveness** — success rate, correctness, completion
- L2 **memory quality** — precision/recall, **contradiction rate, staleness, coverage**
- L3 **efficiency** — latency, prompt tokens, retrieval calls, storage growth
- L4 **governance** — privacy leakage, **deletion compliance**, access violations

**Write-path engineering checklist** `[V]`: filtering → canonicalization (normalize dates, names, quantities) → deduplication → priority scoring → metadata tagging (timestamp, source, task label, confidence). "The optimal filtering threshold is application-specific."

**Read path** `[V]`: two-stage retrieval (fast BM25 → slow reranker), retrieval-or-not gating, token budgeting, cache layers. Guidance: **"retrieving a handful of highly relevant passages into a moderate-length context often beats both pure long-context and pure retrieval approaches."** Retrieval overhead is quoted as **200–500 ms typical**.

**Staleness/contradiction mechanisms** `[V]`: temporal versioning (prefer newest), **source attribution (user statement > agent inference)** — a rule you should hard-code — contradiction detection with flag-for-resolution, periodic consolidation. Their worked risk example: *"A personal assistant that sends a birthday card to a user's ex-partner at the old address is not just unhelpful—it is harmful."*

**Three deployment patterns** `[V]`: (A) monolithic context — prototyping only; (B) **context + retrieval — "production workhorse: coding assistants, customer service, enterprise copilots"**; (C) tiered + RL-learned control — *"Only graduate here when empirical data justify learned control."*

**Observability** `[V]` — the section most relevant to shipping: log every write/read/update/delete with context; **replay tools** to re-run failures with modified memory; **"memory diff"** showing what changed between turns; regression tests for memory behavior. Their diagnosis of the core pain: *"When an agent gives a wrong answer, was the problem in retrieval (wrong records surfaced), in the write path (relevant information never stored), in compression (detail lost during summarization), or in the LLM's reasoning?"*

**Open problems** `[V]` (10): principled consolidation (they propose **"dual-buffer consolidation"** — a probation period before promotion to long-term store); causally grounded retrieval; trustworthy reflection (self-reinforcing error, over-generalization); learning to forget; multimodal/embodied; multi-agent governance; memory-efficient architectures; deeper neuroscience (spreading activation, **memory reconsolidation theory** — retrieval renders memory labile and revisable; Ebbinghaus/spaced repetition); foundation models for memory management; standardized evaluation. Also flagged: **when memories leak into fine-tuned weights, external deletion is insufficient — "machine unlearning is the only path, and it remains far from production-ready."** Directly relevant to your GDPR erasure cascade.

**"From Storage to Experience: A Survey on the Evolution of LLM Agent Memory Mechanisms"** — arXiv:2605.06716, Luo, Tian, Cao, Luo, Lin, Li, Kong, Yang, Ma. Submitted **7 May 2026**, **accepted to ACL 2026 Findings**. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06716 `[V]`
Three-stage evolutionary framework: **Storage (trajectory preservation) → Reflection (trajectory refinement) → Experience (trajectory abstraction)**. Three drivers: long-range consistency, dynamic environments, continual learning. Two frontier mechanisms in the Experience stage: **proactive exploration** and **cross-trajectory abstraction**.

Also noted `[V]`: **"A Survey on the Security of Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents: Toward Mnemonic Sovereignty"** (arXiv:2604.16548), covering the attack surface and defenses 2023–2026; and **"Governing Evolving Memory in LLM Agents … (SSGM)"** (arXiv:2603.11768, Lam et al., 12 Mar 2026) — a governance architecture that **decouples memory evolution from execution** via consistency verification, temporal decay modeling, and access control *prior to* consolidation, plus a taxonomy of memory-corruption risks.

### 6c. Memory consolidation / self-evolving memory — 2026 (your nightly job)

This is a very active area in 2026. The ones that matter for you, in priority order:

**"Retain or Consolidate? Budget-Dependent Operator Selection for Language Agent Memory"** — arXiv:2607.17545, Kang, Liu, Kai, Liang, Tang, Cui, Zhong, Yuan. Submitted **20 July 2026**. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17545 `[V]`
The most directly useful consolidation paper. Central claim: **neither retention nor consolidation is universally preferable — the right operator is a function of budget pressure.** They decompose operator utility into a **coverage effect** (evidence that retention *cannot* fit the budget) and a **signed replacement effect** (impact on raw evidence that already fits). **OAS (Offline Abstraction-Safety)** is "a lightweight learner that estimates action utilities from pre-generation features with held-out harm calibration" — i.e. you can predict, *before* spending the LLM call, whether consolidating a given cluster will help or hurt. Operators evaluated: **retain, merge, abstract (cross-note), rewrite (local)**. Results: on LongMemEval, **consolidation improves accuracy by up to 48% under tight budgets**; retention wins under loose budgets; **cross-note abstraction and merging beat local rewriting whenever compression is needed**. LoCoMo replicates the crossover at smaller thresholds.

**"TRUSTMEM: Learning Trustworthy Memory Consolidation for LLM Agents with Long-Term Memory"** — arXiv:2606.25161, Yang, Paul, Srinivasan, Kulkarni, Chappidi (Samsung-affiliated author set). Submitted **23 June 2026**. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25161 `[V]`
Directly maps onto a human review queue. A **Memory Transition Verifier** scores every candidate update on three axes — **coverage** (did we retain what mattered), **preservation** (did we damage existing correct memory), **faithfulness** (did we invent anything unsupported). Preference pairs among candidate updates then drive **preference-guided RL** over write/revise/delete behavior. Error taxonomy and reductions vs strongest baselines: **omission −40.1%, corruption −79.1%, hallucination −50.0%**. SOTA on MemoryAgentBench; **+12.14 F1 on HaluMem** memory extraction; also validated on Mem-alpha.

**"RecMem: Recurrence-based Memory Consolidation…"** — arXiv:2605.16045, Dai, Deng, Guan, Tian, Yao, Yan, Cheng. Submitted **15 May 2026**, **ACL 2026 Findings**. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16045 `[V]`
The cost-control answer. Existing systems invoke an LLM on **every** interaction to extract memory. RecMem instead writes raw interactions into a **"subconscious memory"** layer encoded with cheap embeddings, and **only fires the LLM when sustained recurrence appears across semantically similar interactions** — the reasoning being that a recurring semantic cluster is where the information density is. A semantic-refinement pass recovers fine-grained facts the extractor dropped. **Reduces memory-construction token cost of three SOTA memory systems by up to 87%** while exceeding their accuracy. (Exact recurrence threshold/clustering method isn't in the abstract.)

**"TiMem: Temporal-Hierarchical Memory Consolidation for Long-Horizon Conversational Agents"** — arXiv:2601.02845, Li, Yu, Ni, Zeng, Xu, Zhang, Li, Sang, Duan, Wang, Liu, Tan. Submitted **6 Jan 2026**, revised 30 Apr 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02845 `[V]`
A **Temporal Memory Tree (TMT)** consolidating from raw observations up to abstracted persona representations. Three properties: temporal-hierarchical organization; **semantic-guided consolidation across hierarchy levels without fine-tuning**; complexity-aware recall balancing precision and efficiency. **LoCoMo 75.30%** with a **52.20% reduction in recalled memory length**; **LongMemEval-S 76.88%**. Code on GitHub.

**"Episodic-to-Semantic Consolidation Without Identity Drift"** — arXiv:2607.01988, Qin, Luan, Yang, Li. Submitted **2 July 2026**. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01988 `[V]`
Consolidation as a **deterministic function `f: M^ep → M^sem`**, with the semantic layer held *outside* the agent's identity hash so the agent stays "byte-equal across its operational lifetime" while knowledge accumulates. Formal proof of identity invariance via a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set; deterministic aggregation producing **auditable database rows with confidence scores and event provenance**. **79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%], 10 seeds)** vs a Bayesian-shrunk baseline. The *auditable-rows-with-provenance* output shape is a good template for a reviewable consolidation job.

**Others worth knowing** `[V]`:
- **MemSkill** (arXiv:2602.02474, Zhang et al., 2 Feb 2026, rev. 24 May) — reframes memory ops as **learnable, evolvable "memory skills"**: reusable routines for **extracting, consolidating, and pruning**. Architecture = **Controller** (selects skills) + **Executor** (LLM applies them) + **Designer** (periodically reviews *hard cases* where the selected skill produced incorrect/incomplete memory, and proposes refinements + new skills). Closed loop improves both the selection policy and the skill set. Evaluated on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, ALFWorld. This is Voyager's skill library applied to the memory write path.
- **Live-Evo** (arXiv:2602.02369) — decouples experience from usage via **Experience and Meta-Guideline Banks**, with online **experience weights** reinforcing helpful entries and down-weighting stale ones. **+20.8% Brier score** on live financial benchmarks.
- **EvolveMem** (arXiv:2605.13941) — exposes the **full retrieval configuration as a structured action space** optimized by an LLM diagnosis module; co-evolves stored knowledge *and* retrieval infrastructure. **+25.7% relative on LoCoMo.**
- **AgentHER** (arXiv:2603.21357) — Hindsight Experience Replay for agent trajectories: relabel failed episodes as successes for alternative goals. **+7.6–11.4% across four model families, 2× sample efficiency** vs success-only training.
- **MemMA** (arXiv:2603.18718) — **synthesizes probe QA pairs, verifies the current memory against them, and converts failures into repair actions *before the memory is finalized*.** Plug-and-play across storage backends. This is essentially unit-testing your fact extraction at write time.
- **UMEM** (arXiv:2602.10652) — joint extraction+management with **Semantic Neighborhood Modeling** and a neighborhood-level marginal-utility reward via GRPO; **up to +10.67%**, with monotonic growth under continuous evolution.
- **Darwinian Memory** (arXiv:2601.22528) — training-free memory as an ecosystem under **utility-driven natural selection**, actively pruning suboptimal paths; **+18.0% success, +33.9% execution stability**.
- **SCM: Sleep-Consolidated Memory** (arXiv:2604.20943, Saish Sachin Shinde, 22 Apr 2026) — explicitly a *research preview*. Five components: limited-capacity working memory, multi-dimensional importance tagging, **offline sleep-stage consolidation with distinct NREM and REM phases** (REM creates **synthetic associative linkages**), intentional value-based forgetting, computational self-model. Claims: perfect recall over ten-turn conversations, **90.9% memory-noise reduction** via adaptive forgetting, sub-millisecond search at hundreds of concepts. Treat as directionally interesting; the eval scale is tiny.

**Agentic context engineering (ACE)** — arXiv:2510.04618, Zhang, Hu, Upasani, Ma, Hong, Kamanuru, Rainton, Wu, Ji, Li, Thakker, Zou, Olukotun. Oct 2025, v3. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04618 `[V]`
Not 2026, but the mechanism is the best-argued case against naive LLM rewriting of a memory store, which is exactly what a nightly consolidation job risks doing.
- **Generator** produces reasoning traces; **Reflector** critiques them to extract lessons (optionally multi-iteration); **Curator** synthesizes lessons "into compact delta entries, which are **merged deterministically into the existing context by lightweight, non-LLM logic**."
- **Bullet representation:** each item = **unique identifier + content + counters for how often it was marked helpful or harmful**. Content is "a reusable strategy, domain concept, or common failure mode."
- **Merge:** "Bullets with new identifiers are appended, while existing bullets are updated in place (e.g., incrementing counters)." Multiple deltas merge **in parallel**, enabling batched adaptation.
- **Grow-and-refine:** de-duplication "prunes redundancy by comparing bullets via semantic embeddings," run either **proactively (after each delta) or lazily (only when the context window is exceeded)**.
- **Context collapse, measured:** *"At step 60 the context contained **18,282 tokens** and achieved an accuracy of **66.7**, but at the very next step it collapsed to just **122 tokens**, with accuracy dropping to **57.1** — worse than the baseline accuracy of **63.7**."* One monolithic LLM rewrite destroyed the store.
- **Results:** AppWorld (DeepSeek-V3.1) offline **TGC 76.2% (+12.5)**, **SGC 64.3% (+21.4)**, avg 59.4% (+17.0); online avg 59.5% (+17.1). Finance offline w/ labels: **FiNER 78.3% (+7.6)**, **Formula 85.5% (+18.0)**, avg 81.9% (+12.8). Cost: **−82.3% adaptation latency vs GEPA**, **−75.1% rollouts vs GEPA**, **−83.6% token dollar cost vs Dynamic Cheatsheet**, **91.8% KV-cache reuse at eval (82.6% billed cost reduction)**. Matches the top-ranked production AppWorld agent on overall average and surpasses it on the harder test-challenge split, **using a smaller open-source model**.

Follow-ons `[V]`: **PAACE** (arXiv:2512.16970, plan-aware compression with next-k-task relevance modeling), **M³-ACE** (arXiv:2603.08369, Mar 2026), **SLEUTH** (arXiv:2511.22850), **NightFeats** (arXiv:2606.11199 — adds **temporal-semantic reranking, bounded contradiction reconciliation, citation-preserving composition**).

**MemCube abstraction** `[V]`: Memory Payload (semantic content) + Metadata Header with three field groups:
| Group | Fields | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Descriptive identifiers** | Timestamp, Origin Signature, Semantic Type | identity, classification |
| **Governance attributes** | Access Control (read/write/share), Lifespan Policy (TTL/decay), Priority Level, Compliance Tags | control, security, scheduling |

Provenance API "embed[s] metadata into memory objects at creation or modification time … with a unique provenance ID that persists throughout its lifecycle." The **Version Chain** logs modifications and derivation lineage.

**Three memory types and their migration paths** `[V]`:
- **Plaintext** — external editable knowledge modules (passages, graphs, templates), retrieved at inference.
- **Activation** — KV-cache, hidden states, attention weights; runtime state.
- **Parametric** — model weights / LoRA / adapters; implicit, no retrieval.

Transformations (Fig. 5): **Plaintext → Activation** ("Frequently used plaintext memory can be pre-transformed into activation vectors or attention templates"); **Plaintext/Activation → Parameter** ("Stable knowledge across tasks can be distilled into parameter modules"); **Parameter → Plaintext** ("Cold or outdated parameters can be offloaded into external plaintext storage"). MemScheduler "dynamically adjusts a memory block's tier and format based on usage frequency, contextual dependency, and task fit."

**Three-layer architecture** `[V]`:
- **Interface layer** — **MemReader** (parses NL into a structured `MemoryCall`: task intent, temporal scope, entity focus), **Memory API** (Provenance / Update / LogQuery), **Memory Pipeline** (declarative chaining: retrieve → augment → archive).
- **Operation layer** — **MemOperator** (tagging, KGs, semantic layering; hybrid symbolic + semantic retrieval), **MemScheduler** (type-aware transformation and loading), **MemLifecycle** (state transitions, versioning, expiration).
- **Infrastructure layer** — **MemGovernance** (access control by user/role/model/task, retention, audit logging, compliance), **MemVault** (repositories), **MemLoader/MemDumper** (import/export, cross-platform sync — attacks the "memory islands" problem across ChatGPT/Cursor/etc.), **MemStore** (publish-subscribe for cross-agent memory sharing).

**Lifecycle states** `[V]`: **Generated → Activated → Merged → Archived → Expired**.

**Scheduling policy** `[V]`: coherence-heavy multi-turn tasks favor **KV-cache recall**; procedural/expert flows favor **parametric modules**; factual queries favor **plaintext retrieval + contextualization**. Selection driven by "contextual similarity, access frequency, temporal decay, and priority tags," with a three-layered **topic–concept–fact** task schema for **Task-Aligned Memory Routing**. No explicit "Next-Scene Prediction" lookahead mechanism found in the paper text `[V that it's absent]`.

## What this adds up to for your system

The through-line across the strongest 2026 evidence, stated as implementable positions:

1. **Put the LLM at mutation time, not just at inscription time.** ForgetEval's central result: inscribe-time LLM gets you canonicalization (100% on identifier obfuscation and cross-lingual) but **0% on intent-aware deletion**; a mutation-time hook gets you 78–85% on intent-aware deletion and a **+22.6 to +24.1 pt** overall lift, and **costs nothing on the read path** (recall latency unchanged; ~2.3 s/case on mutations only, ~$0.00044/call). For a nightly job, 2.3 s per mutation is free. (arXiv:2606.15903)
2. **Expose a partial-edit primitive.** Every system without one scores **0/40 on compound_fact** — a single source sentence carrying two facts about different topics, where only one should be superseded. Given you extract *atomic* facts, this is either a solved problem for you or the exact place your extractor will silently fail. (arXiv:2606.15903)
3. **Don't let a nightly LLM rewrite the store monolithically.** ACE's measured collapse — 18,282 tokens → 122 tokens in one step, accuracy 66.7 → 57.1, below the 63.7 no-adaptation baseline — is the failure mode. Use **itemized deltas with stable IDs + helpful/harmful counters, merged by deterministic non-LLM logic**, with embedding-similarity dedup run lazily. (arXiv:2510.04618)
4. **Make consolidation budget-conditional, and prefer merge/abstract over local rewrite.** Consolidation is worth **up to +48%** under tight budgets and *negative* under loose ones; cross-note abstraction and merging beat local rewriting whenever compression is needed. Estimate the utility before spending the call. (arXiv:2607.17545)
5. **Don't run an LLM on every write.** Buffer raw items with cheap embeddings and fire the extractor only on recurring semantic clusters: **up to −87% memory-construction token cost** with *higher* accuracy. This is the natural shape for a nightly job over a day's inbound email/meetings. (arXiv:2605.16045)
6. **Verify every proposed mutation on three axes before it lands** — coverage, preservation, faithfulness. That triple is exactly the schema your human review queue should surface, and it bought **−40.1% omission, −79.1% corruption, −50.0% hallucination**. Pair it with MemMA's trick of synthesizing probe QA pairs and verifying the memory against them *before finalizing*. (arXiv:2606.25161, arXiv:2603.18718)
7. **Your retrieval should be query→triple, not query→entity.** +12.5 avg recall points over NER-to-node and +27.5 over query-to-node — by far the largest single lever in HippoRAG 2. Seed PPR with ≤5 phrase nodes scored by average filtered-triple score, plus *all* passage nodes at **weight 0.05**, damping **0.5**, synonym-edge threshold **0.8**. The LLM triple filter is worth only **+0.7 points** — deprioritize or make it async. (arXiv:2502.14802)
8. **Benchmark your forgetting, not just your recall — the rankings invert.** MemPalace: 0% on ForgetEval-Adv, 40% on the recall benchmark. DMR/LoCoMo-style suites will not catch a system that never forgets. ForgetEval is MIT-licensed and the Adapter Protocol is six methods — you could wire your knowledge package to it in an afternoon. (arXiv:2606.15903)
9. **Hard-code source precedence and temporal versioning:** user statement > agent inference; prefer newest; flag contradictions rather than auto-resolving. And note the survey's warning that once memories leak into fine-tuned weights, external deletion is insufficient — relevant to your GDPR erasure cascade if you ever distill facts into a model. (arXiv:2603.07670)

**One caveat to carry forward:** the ForgetEval paper is transparent that 253/385 adversarial cases were drafted by DeepSeek-V3, admitted by a single Qwen-2.5-72B judge, *and* the winning hook is also DeepSeek-V3 — the authors say outright they "cannot fully rule out residual overlap." ## 1. Deleting a fact and everything derived from it

### 1.1 The database-theory foundation: provenance semirings

**[V]** Green, Karvounarakis, Tannen, *Provenance Semirings*, PODS 2007 — https://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/pods07.pdf (also https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1265530.1265535)

Annotate each base tuple with a variable from a commutative semiring $(K, +, \times, 0, 1)$ and propagate annotations through the query:
- $\times$ = **joint use** (conjunction / join) — you needed *both*.
- $+$ = **alternative use** (union / projection / disjunction) — *either* would do.

The hierarchy, coarsest → finest **[V]**:

| Semiring | What it computes | Cascade power |
|---|---|---|
| `B` (booleans) | did it derive at all | none |
| `N` (naturals, bag semantics) | # of derivation paths | counting only |
| `Lineage(X)` | **flat set** of contributing source tuples | ⚠️ cannot distinguish AND from OR |
| `Why(X)` | set of *witness sets* | knows alternative supports |
| `PosBool(X)` | positive boolean formula | correct survival test |
| `Trio(X)` | witnesses with multiplicity | + counting |
| `N[X]` (**how-provenance**, polynomials) | most general; all others are homomorphic images | full |

**The operationally decisive result [V]:** to answer *"does derived tuple $t$ survive if I delete source $s$?"*, take $t$'s how-provenance polynomial, **set the variable for $s$ to 0, and evaluate**. $t$ survives iff the polynomial is non-zero — i.e. iff some monomial (alternative derivation) has no deleted variable in it. `PosBool(X)` is the coarsest semiring that still answers this correctly; **`Lineage(X)` (a flat set) does not**, because a set loses whether the members were joint or alternative supports.

> **This is a live bug class in your schema.** Your `facts.derivedFrom: ObjectId[]` (packages/knowledge/schemas/facts.ts:44) is exactly `Lineage(X)`. If a consolidated fact was produced by **merging two corroborating facts** (disjunctive — survives if one parent survives) it is indistinguishable from one produced by **joining two complementary facts** (conjunctive — must die if either parent dies). Erasing one parent then either over-deletes or under-deletes, and Art. 17 makes under-deletion the expensive failure.

**Minimal fix that buys correct cascade semantics without full `N[X]`:** store DNF instead of a flat set —
```ts
// derivedFrom as PosBool(X) in DNF: outer array = alternative derivations (+),
// inner array = jointly-required parents (×). Survives iff ∃ monomial with no erased parent.
derivedFrom: z.array(z.array(zodObjectId).min(1)).min(1).optional()
```
Or, cheaper: keep the flat array and add a discriminator `derivation: "merge" | "corroboration" | "inference" | "summary"`, with a documented per-kind cascade rule. `"corroboration"` → survive-if-any (rewrite text, drop the erased parent, recompute confidence); everything else → delete-if-any.

### 1.2 Deletion propagation is NP-hard in general — so pick your objective

**[V-snippet]** Buneman, Khanna, Tan, *On the Propagation of Deletions and Annotations through Views*, PODS 2002, pp.150–158 — https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/on-the-propagation-of-deletions-and-annotations-through-views/ · https://www.academia.edu/681183/On_Propagation_of_Deletions_and_Annotations_Through_Views

Two distinct optimisation objectives, and they conflict:
- **Source side-effect:** delete the minimum number of *input* tuples to remove view tuple $t$.
- **View side-effect:** delete input tuples so that the minimum number of *other output* tuples collaterally die.

They prove a **dichotomy**: for queries in the same class, each objective is either in P or NP-hard. **[V-snippet]** Follow-ups: *Multi-Tuple Deletion Propagation* (Kimelfeld et al.) http://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/user/dwoodruf/www/kvw13.pdf ; *New Results on the Complexity of Deletion Propagation* https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-57602-8_30 ; a 2025 unified treatment, Gatterbauer & Simons, *A unified and practical approach to Generalized Deletion Propagation* https://gatterbauer.name/download/Gatterbauer-Simons2025-Generalized-Deletion-Propagation.pdf

**Practical takeaway:** don't try to be optimal. For GDPR you are **not** solving the optimisation problem — you are solving the *forced* problem: the erasure target is given, and you must take the transitive closure. Optimality only matters if you want to minimise collateral damage to unrelated facts, and there the answer is "make your provenance finer-grained (§1.1) so there is less collateral damage by construction."

### 1.3 The AI-side equivalent: Truth Maintenance Systems

**[V]** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason_maintenance

- **JTMS** (Doyle 1979): each belief node carries **justifications** (in-list, out-list) and an `IN`/`OUT` label. A node is `IN` iff it has at least one *valid* justification. Retracting a premise flips it `OUT`, and **dependency-directed backtracking** walks only the affected sub-network rather than recomputing everything.
- **ATMS** (de Kleer 1986): each node carries a **label** = minimal set of *environments* (assumption sets) under which it holds — this is literally `Why(X)`/DNF provenance, and it lets you answer "which facts survive under which surviving sources" for all subsets at once.

**Why you care:** a JTMS is the right mental model for the nightly consolidation job. Consolidated facts are *derived nodes*; source documents are *premises*. When a premise is retracted (Art. 17), you re-label the dependency network rather than re-running consolidation from scratch. `derivedFrom` **is** the justification edge — you already have the graph, you just need the label semantics.

### 1.4 Concrete cascade algorithm for your schema

```
erasePerson(personId):
  1. FRONTIER  := sources whose PII cannot be redacted away (audio/attachments), 
                  plus facts anchored to personId
  2. Hard-delete frontier facts.
  3. FIXPOINT loop (bounded, with a visited-set to kill cycles):
       for each fact F with F.derivedFrom ∩ deletedIds ≠ ∅:
          if derivation is conjunctive  -> delete F, add to deletedIds
          if disjunctive and ∃ surviving monomial -> rewrite F.text without the
             erased parent, drop the parent id, recompute confidence, mark
             `provenanceRepaired: true`
          else -> delete F
     repeat until no change (depth cap ~8, then alert)
  4. Drop derived caches wholesale (dossiers) — cheaper and safer than surgery;
     they rebuild lazily. (You already do this. Good.)
  5. Redact retained audit artefacts (proposals) rather than deleting them.
     (You already do this. Good — see §2.4 on why retention of the audit trail
     is defensible under Art. 17(3)(e).)
  6. Flag sources with no surviving facts for blob deletion; two-phase with
     `blobsPendingDeletion` + `markSourceBlobsDeleted`. (You already do this.
     This is the correct crash-safe pattern.)
  7. Emit an append-only erasure receipt (see §2.6).
```

**Gap in the current implementation worth checking:** step 3 (transitive `derivedFrom` closure) — your `ErasureReport` reports `factsDeleted` but the consolidation job creates facts whose `derivedFrom` may reference facts anchored to *other* people while still containing the erased person's text. A merged fact "Anna and Petra both objected to the Q3 timeline" is anchored to Anna, derived from a Petra fact, and *still names Petra*. The name-token redactor handles the text, but the fact document itself survives with a dangling `derivedFrom` pointer. **Recommend:** run the redactor over `facts.text` too, and validate `derivedFrom` referential integrity post-erasure.

## 2. GDPR Art. 17 for RAG / vector stores / memory systems

### 2.1 What the law actually says about derived copies

**[V]** Article 17(2) GDPR — https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/ — a controller who has *made the data public* must take "reasonable steps, including technical measures, to inform controllers which are processing the personal data" that the subject requested erasure of **"any links to, or copies or replications of, those personal data."**

**[V]** Recital 66 verbatim — https://gdpr-info.eu/recitals/no-66/ :
> "To strengthen the right to be forgotten in the online environment, the right to erasure should also be extended in such a way that a controller who has made the personal data public should be obliged to inform the controllers which are processing such personal data to erase any links to, or copies or replications of those personal data."

**[V]** Article 19 GDPR verbatim — https://gdpr-info.eu/art-19-gdpr/ :
> "The controller shall communicate any rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing carried out in accordance with Article 16, Article 17(1) and Article 18 to each recipient to whom the personal data have been disclosed, unless this proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort."

**Interpretation for your system.** Art. 17(2)/Recital 66 is about *external* controllers and only bites when you published the data. But **internally there is no "derived data" exemption at all** — embeddings, summaries, consolidated facts, dossiers, and search indexes are all *your* processing of *the same* personal data. If they still relate to an identified/identifiable person, Art. 17(1) reaches them directly. The "copies or replications" language is the strongest textual hook, and it is why "we deleted the source document but kept the summary" is not a defensible position.

**[V]** Art. 17(3) exemptions that matter to you: compliance with a legal obligation; archiving/research/statistics under Art. 89 where erasure would seriously impair the purpose; and **"establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims"** — this is the usual basis for retaining a *redacted* audit trail of the erasure itself.

### 2.2 Are embeddings personal data? — Yes, presumptively, and 2025–26 case law sharpens it

**[V]** **EDPB Opinion 28/2024** (adopted 17 Dec 2024) — official PDF https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2024-12/edpb_opinion_202428_ai-models_en.pdf ; readable summaries **[V]** https://securiti.ai/summary-of-edpb-opinion-282024-concerning-ai-models-processing-of-personal-data/ and **[V-snippet]** https://www.hunton.com/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/edpb-publishes-opinion-on-processing-of-personal-data-in-the-context-of-ai-models

The **two-pronged anonymity test** for an AI model **[V]** — anonymity requires it be *very unlikely* both to:
1. "directly or indirectly extract the personal data of individuals whose data was used to create the model", **and**
2. "extract such personal data from the model through queries"

...assessed against **"all means reasonably likely to be used"** by the controller *or another person*, case-by-case. The EDPB explicitly acknowledges personal data may be embedded in model parameters as **mathematical objects** — i.e. *being a vector does not launder personal data*. **[V]** Also: facilitating "the right to erasure and the right to opt-out" is listed as a **mitigating measure** in the legitimate-interest balancing test — building good erasure is legally load-bearing, not just hygiene.

**[V]** The three unlawful-development scenarios: (1) same controller — SA can order deletion of the unlawfully-processed data, tainting downstream Art. 6(1)(f) reliance; (2) different controller — SA assesses both; (3) genuinely anonymised before deployment — subsequent processing escapes GDPR.

**[V-snippet]** **CJEU, *EDPS v SRB*, C-413/23 P, judgment 4 Sep 2025** — https://curia.europa.eu/site/upload/docs/application/pdf/2025-09/cp250107en.pdf ; analyses: https://fpf.org/blog/rethinking-personal-data-the-cjeus-contextual-turn-in-edps-vs-srb/ · https://www.taylorwessing.com/en/insights-and-events/insights/2025/09/analysis-of-the-cjeu-judgment · https://www.skadden.com/insights/publications/2025/11/in-a-landmark-decision-eu-court-clarifies

Holding: "personal" is **relative, not absolute**. The *same* pseudonymised data can be non-personal for a recipient without the key while remaining personal for the sender. Classification depends on whether *that* recipient can reasonably re-identify, weighing technical, organisational and legal factors. **Also held: personal opinions/views are personal data because they are "necessarily closely linked" to the person** — directly relevant to a system that stores *"Petra objects to the Q3 timeline"* as an atomic fact.

**Practical read for a fact store:** your facts are opinion-bearing statements about identified people. They are unambiguously personal data. Embeddings of them are pseudonymised personal data *for you* (you hold the mapping). The relative approach only helps you if you ship vectors to a third party without the key — it does **not** help you internally.

**[V-snippet]** EDPB **Guidelines 01/2025 on Pseudonymisation** (adopted 16 Jan 2025) — https://www.hunton.com/insights/publications/edpb-advises-on-pseudonymisation-for-gdpr-compliance · https://www.stibbe.com/publications-and-insights/key-takeaways-and-insights-from-the-edpb-pseudonymisation-guidelines — pseudonymisation ≠ anonymisation; pseudonymised data remains personal data for anyone holding or able to obtain the additional information. **[V-snippet]** EDPB published a *Report on Stakeholder Event on Anonymisation and Pseudonymisation* on **18 Feb 2026**, feeding into forthcoming anonymisation guidance — https://www.insideprivacy.com/gdpr/edpb-publishes-report-on-stakeholder-event-on-anonymisation-and-pseudonymisation/ ⚠️ *anonymisation guidance is still in flight as of your "today"; re-check before relying on it.*

### 2.3 Soft-delete is **not** erasure — the empirical proof (2026)

**[V]** *Ghost Vectors: Soft-Deleted Embeddings Remain Reconstructible in HNSW Vector Databases* — https://arxiv.org/html/2606.18497v1 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.18497)

This paper is the reason to design your deletion path defensively. Threat model: adversary with **read access to raw storage** (insider, cloud misconfig, or **backup exposure**), knows the embedding model, has no keys or API access.

Attack **[V]**: pull vectors straight off disk (`hnswlib.get_items()` on ChromaDB, `index.reconstruct_n()` on FAISS), run an **off-the-shelf Vec2Text corrector with no fine-tuning**, then NER the reconstructed text. One inference step reaches 98.4% of plateau quality at **30.7 ms/record**.

Recovery rates **[V]**:

| Corpus | Metric | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| Wikipedia biographies (n=98) | person names recovered | **25.5%** |
| Wikipedia biographies | geographic locations | **46.4%** |
| Synthetic clinical (n=1000) | patient surname | **49.9%** |
| Synthetic clinical | gender | 73.4% |
| Synthea EHR (n=1000) | age/gender markers | 100% (ROUGE-L 0.290) |
| LFW faces (n=4324) | top-1 identity | **99.17%** |

Per-store behaviour **[V]**: **ChromaDB** marks deletion in SQLite metadata while `index.bin` is *physically unchanged*; **FAISS** `IndexHNSWFlat` has no `delete()` at all — vectors "accumulate indefinitely"; **Weaviate 1.26.6 embedded** grew on disk after deletion (52.5 MB → 55.4 MB) because "deletion appends metadata instead." Not tested: Milvus, Qdrant, pgvector, Pinecone.

Mitigation that worked **[V]**: **epoch key rotation** — AES-256-CTR per epoch, irreversibly discard the key on deletion. Reduced PII recovery to **0%** (ROUGE-L 0.000 across 500 records) at ~**0.005 ms/record** (2.5 ms for 500), and emits an **ECDSA-signed deletion proof π**. Mitigations that **failed**: orthogonal transforms (attacker applies Tᵀ), differential privacy (noise that kills recovery kills utility; recovery still ROUGE-L ≈0.073), query-side transforms (reversible at storage layer). Full index rebuild works (2,250 ms) but is **not retroactive** to backups.

Legal framing they use **[V]**: Art. 17(1) + EDPB Guidelines 05/2019 — erasure must be **verifiable and irreversible**; "an API returning no records can mean either deletion or suppression." Art. 5(1)(e) storage limitation; Art. 5(2) accountability (signed proofs); Art. 9 special-category. They coin **"compliance debt"** = one recoverable record per un-reclaimed soft delete.

### 2.4 Vector store operational reality: tombstones and compaction

**[V]** https://milvus.io/ai-quick-reference/how-do-delete-operations-or-updates-in-a-vector-database-affect-storage-usage-over-time-... — deletes mark vectors invalid/tombstoned; **compaction** later "consolidates fragmented data by rewriting valid vectors into new storage blocks and discarding deleted or outdated ones," rebuilding indexes as needed. Trigger thresholds are implementation-specific; some engines require manual compaction.

**[V-snippet]** HNSW supports incremental insert but **not** true delete; the standard workaround is soft-delete + periodic compaction, and index quality degrades over time. Rule of thumb quoted: **reindex when the deletion ratio exceeds 10–15%**. Measured compaction/vacuum costs on a delete+reinsert workload: **pgvector ~53 s VACUUM, Milvus ~11 s compaction** — https://sukruyusufkaya.com/en/blog/vektor-veritabani-secimi-2026-pgvector-qdrant (and https://aimultiple.com/open-source-vector-databases). ⚠️ these are third-party benchmark figures on unspecified hardware; treat as order-of-magnitude.

> **Your architecture already dodges most of this.** `facts.embedding` is an inline array on the fact document, not a row in an external HNSW index. `deleteOne` on the fact removes the embedding atomically in the same operation. If you later move to Atlas Vector Search, the index is derived from the collection via the mongot change stream, so document deletion propagates — but you inherit *tombstone/compaction* semantics inside mongot's Lucene segments **[R]**, and you should add a post-erasure **verification query** (search for the erased person's name/embedding, assert 0 hits) rather than trusting the delete ack.

### 2.6 Crypto-shredding — the strongest available primitive, and it works in MongoDB

**[V]** MongoDB official: *Implementing Right to Erasure with CSFLE* — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/csfle/tutorials/right-to-erasure/

Pattern: **one Data Encryption Key (DEK) per data subject**, `key_alt_names=[userId]`. User doc stores `dek_id`. Encryption references the DEK by `key_alt_name`. Erasure = `db.keyvault.delete_one({_id: user_dek_id})`. Ciphertext stays; decryption fails with `EncryptionError("not all keys requested were satisfied")`.

Caveats the docs state explicitly **[V]**:
- **Client DEK cache TTL is 60 seconds** — decryption can still succeed for up to a minute after key deletion.
- **Key vault must live on a separate cluster** from the data, so restoring a data backup does not resurrect deleted DEKs.
- Oplog/transaction logs are **not** addressed by crypto-shredding.
- MongoDB explicitly disclaims: *"MongoDB provides no guarantees that the solution and techniques described in this article fulfill all regulatory requirements around the right to erasure."*
- **They recommend defence-in-depth: delete the encrypted data too.** Crypto-shredding is the backstop for the copies you can't reach (backups, oplog, snapshots).
- Algorithms: `AEAD_AES_256_CBC_HMAC_SHA_512_Deterministic` (searchable) vs `_Random` (stronger). Queryable Encryption crypto-shredding is **not** covered by that page.

**[V-snippet]** Regulator recognition of cryptographic erasure as valid RTBF implementation — EDPB Guidelines 5/2019, UK ICO, CNIL — provided strong algorithm (AES-256), irreversible key destruction, auditable — https://granit-fx.dev/blog/crypto-shredding-gdpr-erasure-without-deleting-rows/ · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crypto-shredding · https://medium.com/@brentrobinson5/crypto-shredding-how-it-can-solve-modern-data-retention-challenges-da874b01745b · https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-17-how-to-set-up-crypto-shredding-for-gdpr-right-to-erasure-compliance-in-google-cloud/view ⚠️ the specific attribution of endorsement to each of those three regulators is from a vendor blog; verify against the primary guidelines before citing to a DPO.

**MongoDB-specific residue you should document [R, unverified]:** `deleteOne` does not zero WiredTiger pages (space is reclaimed lazily, or on compact/initial-sync); the **oplog** retains the delete and, if `changeStreamPreAndPostImages` is enabled on `facts`/`sources`, retains the **full pre-image** of erased documents for the configured expiry; Atlas **continuous/snapshot backups** retain erased documents for the whole retention window. → Actions: (a) confirm pre/post-images are **off** for PII-bearing collections, (b) set backup retention **shorter than your published erasure SLA**, or document the deferred-erasure-of-backups position, (c) note oplog window in your Art. 30 records.

## 3. Right-to-be-forgotten in knowledge graphs

### 3.1 Invalidation vs. deletion — the bitemporal pattern (Zep/Graphiti)

**[V]** https://www.getzep.com/ai-agents/temporal-knowledge-graph/ and **[V]** Zep paper, arXiv:2501.13956, *Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory*, Rasmussen/Paliychuk/Beauvais/Ryan/Chalef, 20 Jan 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956

Four timestamps per edge **[V]**:
- `valid_at` / **valid from** — when the fact became true in the world
- `invalid_at` / **valid to** — when it stopped being true (open if current)
- **observed** — when the source stated it
- `created_at` / **recorded** — when the system ingested it (provenance)

Plus `expired_at` **[V-snippet]** — internal system time for versioning and **logical deletion** (https://neo4j.com/blog/developer/graphiti-knowledge-graph-memory/ · https://deepwiki.com/getzep/graphiti).

Semantics **[V]**: *"When new information contradicts an existing fact, the system closes the old fact's validity window (sets 'valid to') rather than deleting it."* Superseded facts are **closed, not deleted, so the history stays auditable.** Retrieval filters by the validity window at query time. Zep benchmarks **[V]**: DMR 94.8% vs MemGPT 93.4%; up to **18.5%** LongMemEval accuracy improvement; **90%** latency reduction.

> **The critical distinction for you:** bitemporal invalidation is a *quality* mechanism (truth changed), **not** an erasure mechanism (subject withdrew). Your `supersededBy` + `validUntil` (facts.ts:47–53, `currentlyValidFilter`) is exactly Graphiti's closure pattern and is correct for the dream cycle. **It must not be reused for Art. 17.** Erasure needs `deleteOne`, not `$set: { validUntil }`. Keep two distinct verbs — this is the same lesson as §5.6's `release` (soft) vs `purge` (hard).

### 3.2 Tombstoning, orphan cleanup, and event-sourced stores

**[V-snippet]** Event-sourcing tombstone pattern (Sequent) — https://sequent.io/docs/concepts/gdpr.html — apply a **Tombstone Event** to all aggregates belonging to a user; the tombstone event **propagates** to other aggregates that must scrub identifiable data from their event streams. This is the right shape if you ever move `proposals` to an append-only log: you cannot delete history, so you emit a scrub event and rewrite projections.

**[V-snippet]** Kafka tombstones + log compaction — https://medium.com/@DevBox_rohitrawat/kafka-tombstone-messages-explained... — null-valued record for a key; compaction eventually removes prior values. Note the **eventual** — same "when is it actually gone?" problem as HNSW compaction.

**[V-snippet]** Cassandra tombstones raise the same GDPR concern (deletion marker ≠ deletion) — https://tantusdata.com/insights/gdpr-the-forgotten-done-right/

**[V-snippet]** Cascade + orphan semantics in KG maintenance: automatic propagation of **1-hop edge removal and orphan node elimination** when nodes/edges are deleted, with the option of re-linking orphans to preserve connectivity (CleanGraph, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.03932 ; also a USPTO patent on KG node expiration, https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10725982).

**[V-snippet]** Graph unlearning (GNN weight-level, adjacent to your problem but not your problem): *Graph Unlearning: Efficient Node Removal in GNNs* https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.04785 ; *Forget and Explain: Transparent Verification of GNN Unlearning* https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.07450 — the latter is interesting for its framing: **verify unlearning by diffing pre- and post-deletion explanation snapshots**. That verification idea transfers directly: snapshot the dossier/search results for the erased person before and after, and assert the diff is total.

**Orphan classes to sweep in your schema:**
- `sources` with zero surviving facts → blob deletion (you handle this)
- `people`/`organizations`/`engagements` with zero surviving facts and no other anchor → orphan entity
- `facts.derivedFrom` pointing at deleted `_id`s → dangling justification
- `dossiers` referencing deleted entity ids → you drop wholesale (correct)
- Atlas Search index entries → verify, don't assume

We approach the construction of unlearned knowledge as a constrained optimization problem, deriving two key components... particularly effective for closed-source LLMs, where existing unlearning methods often fail."* Evaluated on ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama-2-7b-chat, PaLM 2 against **five criteria: effectiveness, universality, harmlessness, simplicity, robustness.** Extends to multimodal LLMs and LLM-based agents. ⚠️ the abstract names but does not define the "two key components"; I could not retrieve the body.

**Important nuance this paper exposes and that applies to you:** their approach is *behavioural* — they **inject retrieval-time instructions** to suppress the answer rather than only deleting the record. **[V-snippet]** **MUSE benchmark** — Shi et al., arXiv:2407.06460 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.06460 · https://blog.genlaw.org/pdfs/genlaw_icml2024/82.pdf · code https://github.com/jaechan-repo/muse_bench · https://openreview.net/forum?id=TArmA033BU

Six desiderata: **(1) no verbatim memorisation, (2) no knowledge memorisation, (3) no privacy leakage, (4) utility preservation on retained data, (5) scalability w.r.t. removal-request size, (6) sustainability over sequential requests.** Scale: 6.5M-token corpora (Harry Potter books, news), 8 algorithms on 7B models. **Headline finding [V-snippet]:** most algorithms suppress verbatim and knowledge memorisation to some degree, but **only one avoids severe privacy leakage**, and existing algorithms **degrade general utility and cannot sustain successive unlearning requests**.

> **The strategic conclusion for your project:** weight-level unlearning is not usable in production in 2026 — desiderata (5) and (6) are precisely what an ongoing GDPR erasure stream demands, and they are exactly what fails. **Therefore: never put personal facts into weights.** Keep all subject-linked knowledge in MongoDB where erasure is a `deleteOne`, and treat the LLM as a stateless renderer over retrieved context. This is also Ingenire's pitfall #1 (§2.5). Your architecture already does this — it is your single biggest compliance asset and worth writing down explicitly in the DPIA.

## 5. Intentional forgetting for QUALITY — the actual formulas

### 5.1 Generative Agents (Park et al., UIST 2023) — verbatim

**[V]** https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2304.03442 (paper: arXiv:2304.03442; ACM DOI 10.1145/3586183.3606763 — dl.acm.org returns 403 to fetchers)

Quoted verbatim from the paper:
- **Score:** `score = α_recency · recency + α_importance · importance + α_relevance · relevance`
- **Weights:** *"In our implementation, all αs are set to 1."*
- **Recency decay:** *"Our decay factor is 0.995."* — exponential decay over **sandbox game hours since the memory was last retrieved** (note: *last retrieved*, not created — retrieval refreshes recency, which is the spacing effect).
- **Importance prompt (verbatim):** *"On the scale of 1 to 10, where 1 is purely mundane (e.g., brushing teeth, making bed) and 10 is extremely poignant (e.g., a break up, college acceptance), rate the likely poignancy of the following piece of memory."*
- **Relevance:** cosine similarity of query embedding vs memory embedding.
- Each of the three components is **min-max normalised to [0,1]** before summing **[V-snippet]**.
- **Reflection trigger (verbatim):** *"we generate reflections when the sum of the importance scores for the latest events perceived by the agents exceeds a threshold (150 in our implementation). In practice, our agents reflected roughly two or three times a day."*

> **Directly liftable for your nightly job:** the **importance-sum ≥ 150** trigger is a much better consolidation trigger than "run at 3am" — it makes the dream cycle fire proportionally to how much salient material arrived. With your `confidence ∈ [0,1]` you'd want an explicit `importance` field (LLM-rated 1–10) rather than overloading confidence; the two mean different things (importance = how much it matters; confidence = how sure the extractor is).

### 5.2 MemoryBank (Zhong et al., AAAI 2024) — the canonical Ebbinghaus implementation

**[V]** https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2305.10250 (arXiv:2305.10250 ; AAAI https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/29946)

- **Retention:** `R = e^(−t/S)` where `R` = retention fraction, `t` = time elapsed since learning, `S` = memory strength.
- **Init:** `S = 1` on first mention.
- **Reinforcement (verbatim):** *"When a memory item is recalled during conversations, it will persist longer in memory. We increase S by 1 and reset t to 0, hence forget it with a lower probability."*
- **Storage:** three tiers — (a) timestamped detailed conversation logs, (b) **hierarchical summaries**: daily event summaries → global summaries ("bird's eye view"), (c) daily → global **user personality profiles**.
- The authors call it *"an exploratory and highly simplified memory updating model"* based on three Ebbinghaus principles: rate of forgetting, time decay, and the **spacing effect** (retrieval reinforces).

**Note the mechanic that matters:** `S += 1; t := 0` on recall means retention after `n` recalls decays as `e^(−Δt/(1+n))` — a memory recalled 9 times has a 10× longer effective half-life. That is a two-integer implementation (`strength`, `lastRecalledAt`) and needs no ML.

**[V-snippet]** A 2026 follow-up framework paper on Ebbinghaus + LLM context management: https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3803291.3803294 (ICICT 2026). Also *FOREVER: Forgetting Curve-Inspired Memory Replay for LM Continual Learning* arXiv:2601.03938.

### 5.3 SirLLM (ACL 2024) — decay ratio on a key-value cache

**[V-snippet]** arXiv:2405.12528 — https://arxiv.org/html/2405.12528 · https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.143/

- Retains tokens by **Token Entropy**, keeping high-entropy tokens in the KV cache.
- Problem identified: pure top-entropy retention produces **"rigid memory"** — the cache ossifies around a few very-high-entropy tokens and cannot adapt.
- Fix: a **decay ratio `η_decay < 1`**; after each dialogue round the stored entropy cache is **multiplied by `η_decay`**, so old key information naturally fades and recent information dominates.

> **Transferable lesson, independent of KV caches:** *any* purely score-based retention policy ossifies unless you multiplicatively decay the stored scores each cycle. If your consolidation ranks facts by a static importance score, add `score *= η` per nightly run (η ≈ 0.9–0.98) or you will freeze month-one facts in place forever.

### 5.4 A-MEM (NeurIPS 2025) — atomic notes + link generation + memory evolution

**[V]** https://arxiv.org/html/2502.12110v1 (arXiv:2502.12110 ; code https://github.com/agiresearch/a-mem ; NeurIPS 2025 poster https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/119020)

- **Note schema (7 attributes):** `m_i = {c_i, t_i, K_i, G_i, X_i, e_i, L_i}` = content, timestamp, LLM keywords, LLM tags, LLM contextual description, embedding, **linked memories**.
- **Link generation:** cosine `s_{n,j} = (e_n · e_j)/(|e_n||e_j|)`; candidate set `M_near^n = {m_j | rank(s_{n,j}) ≤ k}`; **default k = 10**; then an LLM decides which candidates actually warrant a link based on shared attributes.
- **Memory evolution:** `m_j* ← LLM(m_n ‖ M_near^n \ m_j ‖ m_j ‖ P_s3)` — adding a new note can **rewrite the context/keywords/tags of its existing neighbours**. **No numeric threshold**; the LLM decides via prompt.

> ⚠️ **Erasure hazard you should note:** A-MEM-style *evolution* propagates content from a new note into old notes' `X`/`K`/`G` fields — creating derived copies of personal data with **no recorded provenance edge back to the originating note**. If you adopt any "let new facts rewrite old facts" behaviour in your dream cycle, you **must** append the contributing fact id to the rewritten fact's `derivedFrom`, or the cascade in §1.4 silently misses it. This is the concrete reason your `derivedFrom` refinement matters.

### 5.5 Mem0 (2025) — the ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP control plane

**[V]** https://arxiv.org/html/2504.19413v1 (arXiv:2504.19413, Chhikara et al. 2025)

- **Two phases:** *Extraction* — LLM `φ` over (message pair, conversation summary `S`, recent window) → candidate facts `Ω`. *Update* — retrieve top-`s` semantically similar existing memories, present them plus the candidate to the LLM, which emits a **tool call**.
- **Four operations (verbatim):** `ADD` — *"creation of new memories when no semantically equivalent memory exists"*; `UPDATE` — *"augmentation of existing memories with complementary information"*; `DELETE` — *"removal of memories contradicted by new information"*; `NOOP` — *"when the candidate fact requires no modification."*
- **Config: `s = 10` similar memories, `m = 10` previous messages.**
- **Graph variant `Mem0^g`:** entity extractor + relationship generator → triplets `(v_s, r, v_d)` in Neo4j; conflict detection with an **LLM update resolver** that *"determines if certain relationships should be obsolete, marking them as invalid rather than physically removing them to enable temporal reasoning."*
- **LOCOMO results:** Mem0 66.88% / Mem0^g 68.44% overall (LLM-as-judge); temporal reasoning 58.13 for Mem0^g.
- **Latency (p50/p95, seconds):** Mem0 search 0.148/0.200; Mem0 total 0.708/1.440; Mem0^g total 1.091/2.590; full-context 9.870/17.117 → **91% lower p95**.
- **Tokens/conversation:** Mem0 ~7k, Mem0^g ~14k, full-context ~26k, **Zep >600k**.

> Mem0's `DELETE` is *contradiction-driven quality deletion*, not erasure — the graph variant explicitly marks invalid rather than removing. Same two-verbs lesson again.

### 5.6 ⭐ ForgetEval / Lethe (arXiv:2606.15903, Jun 2026) — the most implementable result

**[V]** https://arxiv.org/html/2606.15903v2

**Five structural families of forgetting:**
| Family | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Supersession** | new fact displaces old; old exits top-k recall |
| **Decay** | released fact (TTL expiry, OTP consumed) stays absent |
| **Amnesia** | forget all facts about one entity; siblings survive (**width control**) |
| **Purge** | hard-delete by identifier — **explicitly framed as GDPR Art. 17** |
| **Drift** | chain of supersessions; intermediates unreachable, only latest wins |

**The protocol (this is a good API to copy).** Mandatory recall plane: `reset()`, `inscribe(text) -> id`, `recall_texts(query, k) -> list[str]`. Optional **control plane**: `supersede(old_query, new_text)`, `release(query) -> int` (soft-delete: TTL/OTP expiry), `purge(query) -> int` (**hard delete by identifier**), and `edit(row_id, new_text)`.

**Lethe's `depth` scalar — the whole lifecycle in one field:**
| value | state |
|---|---|
| `+∞` | **pinned** (permanent retention) |
| `1.0` | **surface** (active, retrievable) |
| `(0,1)` | **sinking** (deprecating, reduced retrieval priority) |
| `0` | **submerged but logged** (out of recall, audit trail preserved) |
| `void` | **erased** (cryptographically deleted) |

Decay is **monotone** (depth only decreases) and every transition appends to an **append-only event table**, enabling time-travel queries and **signed purge receipts** — *"deterministic hashes of purged identifiers logged per mutation timestamp, allowing compliance audits."* The `void` state supports **cryptographic deletion (key-material destruction) on encrypted backends** — i.e. §2.6's crypto-shredding as a lifecycle state.

**Pseudocode [V]:** `Supersede` → BM25-match old row, depth→0, inscribe new at 1.0, reindex vec+FTS5. `Release` → depth 1.0→(0,1). `Purge` → hard-delete matched rows, write purge event with identifier hash, depth→void. `Edit` → update text in place, reindex, **preserve depth**.

**The 10 adversarial attack categories** (385 hand-crafted + LLM-generated cases; scoring is deterministic substring match: pass iff `must_contain ⊆ top-10 blob` AND `must_not_contain ∩ top-10 blob = ∅`):
1. `substring_trap` — must-not substring hidden inside distractor facts
2. `prefix_collision` — `alice@x` vs `alice.smith@x`
3. `paraphrase_supersession` — new fact lexically distant from old
4. `negation_trap` — negated vs affirmative confusion
5. `temporal_qualifier` — date-stamped supersession chains
6. `shared_attribute` — two entities share an attribute; forgetting one must preserve the other (**over-deletion test**)
7. `compound_fact` — one sentence, two topics; partial supersede must preserve the untargeted half
8. `identifier_obfuscation` — same identifier, different surface form (case/whitespace/separators)
9. `cross_lingual_identifier` — same entity in different scripts
10. `recursive_supersession` — chain where the latest state matches an earlier-superseded one

**Results (385 cases):**
| System | Overall |
|---|---|
| Lethe (deterministic) | 244/385 = **63.4%** |
| Mem0 v2.0.2 (`infer=False`) | 263/385 = **68.3%** |
| Mem0 (`infer=True`) | **43.6%** |
| LangGraph InMemoryStore | 242/385 = **62.9%** |
| **Lethe + mutation-time LLM hook** | 353/385 = **91.7%** |
| MemPalace (verbatim retention, no deletion) | **0/385** |
| Graphiti (temporal KG + Neo4j) | 7.0% evaluable / 8.0% strict |
| HippoRAG (KG + PPR) | 9.5% / 8.0% |
| A-MEM | 70.6% / 56.9% |
| Letta / MemGPT | 65.5% / 52.7% |
| OpenMemory | 60.6% / 48.8% |

Per-category standouts: `cross_lingual_identifier` — Lethe **0/38**, LangGraph **1/38**, Mem0 21/38, Lethe+LLM **38/38**. `identifier_obfuscation` — Lethe **2/38** → Lethe+LLM **35/38**. `prefix_collision` — Mem0 only **12/39 (31%)**.

**The three placement regimes (the paper's thesis):**
| Regime | Systems | Strong | Weak |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Deterministic** (no LLM in mutation) | Lethe, LangGraph | lexical/temporal ≥95% | canonicalisation 0–5% |
| **Inscribe-time LLM** | A-MEM, Mem0+v3 | canonicalisation 100% | **intent-aware deletion 0%** |
| **Mutation-time LLM hook** | Lethe+LLM, LangGraph+LLM | deletion precision 78–85%, all categories bright (+22–24 pts) | latency ~2.3 s/case |

The hook uses **three JSON-shaped prompts — `supersede_planner`, `purge_match`, `release_match` — called only at control-plane sites; the recall path stays LLM-free.**

**Headline finding [V]:** *production systems predominantly experience **forgetting** failures rather than recall failures, yet existing benchmarks measure recall.*

**Limitations they state [V]:** ~30% of deterministic failures are substring-scorer artifacts, not real forgetting failures; the hand-crafted layer is English-centric (1–12 cases per script family across 9 scripts); the LLM lift concentrates in 3 categories; n=36–40 per category so aggregate deltas may be noise; `compound_fact` measures edit-primitive presence rather than forgetting per se.

**On cascade/provenance [V]:** *"Not explicitly modeled... cascade semantics and fact provenance are deferred to system design."* `shared_attribute` is the closest proxy — it tests that soft-delete avoids **over-deletion cascades**. So this paper gives you the *primitives and the test suite*; §1 gives you the *cascade semantics* it deliberately leaves out. They compose.

### 5.7 FSFM (arXiv:2604.20300, Apr 2026) — a full forgetting policy with published constants

**[V]** Abstract verbatim from https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20300 — Gu, Xiong, Wang, Ren, Li, Zhang, Guo, Sun, Ma, Shi; v1 22 Apr 2026, v2 23 Apr 2026:

## 6. Synthesis: what I'd actually change in your system

**A. Split the vocabulary into three verbs and never conflate them.** ForgetEval's protocol is the right naming:
- `supersede` — truth changed (dream cycle). You have this: `supersededBy` + `validUntil` + `currentlyValidFilter`. Graphiti-equivalent, correct.
- `release` — quality/TTL soft delete. **You don't have this.** Add a `depth`-like score or `retiredAt` so the consolidation job can demote noise without destroying it.
- `purge` — Art. 17 hard delete. `erasePerson`. **Must be `deleteOne`, must never be expressed as `validUntil`.**

**B. Upgrade `derivedFrom` from `Lineage(X)` to `PosBool(X)`** (§1.1) — DNF nesting or a `derivation` discriminator. Without it your cascade is provably ambiguous on corroboration-merges, which is exactly what a consolidation job produces most of.

**C. Close the transitive-cascade loop in `erasePerson`.** Add the bounded fixpoint over `derivedFrom` (§1.4), run the name redactor over `facts.text` (not just sources/proposals), and add a post-erasure referential-integrity assertion that no surviving `derivedFrom` points at a deleted `_id`.

**D. Add an erasure receipt.** Append-only collection: `{ tenantId, subjectHash (HMAC of identifiers, not the identifiers), requestedAt, completedAt, counts: {facts, sources, proposals, dossiers, blobs}, cascadeDepth, verificationPassed }`. This is ForgetEval's "signed purge receipt" and Ghost Vectors' Art. 5(2) accountability argument, and it's what a DPA will ask for. **Never store the erased person's name in the receipt.**

**E. Verify, don't trust the ack.** After erasure: run an Atlas Search query for the person's name tokens and an embedding kNN for their profile vector, assert zero hits. This is the "deletion audit job" from the aicompetence piece and the pre/post-snapshot diff idea from *Forget and Explain*. Track **time-to-forget** as a metric.

**F. Keep embeddings inline on the fact document.** Your `facts.embedding` design means erasure is atomic with the fact delete. Do **not** move to an external HNSW store without a hard-compaction/crypto-shred story — that is the entire Ghost Vectors result. If you must, use per-tenant (ideally per-subject) key-encrypted vectors with epoch key rotation.

**G. Consider per-person CSFLE DEKs for the highest-risk fields** (`facts.text`, `sources.content`, `sources.email.*`) as the backstop for backups and oplog you cannot reach. Key vault on a **separate cluster**; expect the **60-second DEK cache TTL**; still delete the ciphertext (defence in depth).

**H. Adopt the ForgetEval test cases as your erasure regression suite.** Especially `shared_attribute` (does erasing Anna preserve Petra's facts when they share a source?), `compound_fact` (a fact naming two people), `identifier_obfuscation` and `cross_lingual_identifier` (your redactor already handles German umlauts via Unicode lookarounds — good; but check `Özdemir`/`Oezdemir`/`Ozdemir`, and email-vs-display-name mismatch). ## 1. Deleting a fact and everything derived from it

### 1.1 The database-theory foundation: provenance semirings

**[V]** Green, Karvounarakis, Tannen, *Provenance Semirings*, PODS 2007 — https://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/pods07.pdf (also https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1265530.1265535)

Annotate each base tuple with a variable from a commutative semiring $(K, +, \times, 0, 1)$ and propagate annotations through the query:
- $\times$ = **joint use** (conjunction / join) — you needed *both*.
- $+$ = **alternative use** (union / projection / disjunction) — *either* would do.

The hierarchy, coarsest → finest **[V]**:

| Semiring | What it computes | Cascade power |
|---|---|---|
| `B` (booleans) | did it derive at all | none |
| `N` (naturals, bag semantics) | # of derivation paths | counting only |
| `Lineage(X)` | **flat set** of contributing source tuples | ⚠️ cannot distinguish AND from OR |
| `Why(X)` | set of *witness sets* | knows alternative supports |
| `PosBool(X)` | positive boolean formula | correct survival test |
| `Trio(X)` | witnesses with multiplicity | + counting |
| `N[X]` (**how-provenance**, polynomials) | most general; all others are homomorphic images | full |

**The operationally decisive result [V]:** to answer *"does derived tuple $t$ survive if I delete source $s$?"*, take $t$'s how-provenance polynomial, **set the variable for $s$ to 0, and evaluate**. $t$ survives iff the polynomial is non-zero — i.e. iff some monomial (alternative derivation) has no deleted variable in it. `PosBool(X)` is the coarsest semiring that still answers this correctly; **`Lineage(X)` (a flat set) does not**, because a set loses whether the members were joint or alternative supports.

> **This is a live bug class in your schema.** Your `facts.derivedFrom: ObjectId[]` (packages/knowledge/schemas/facts.ts:44) is exactly `Lineage(X)`. If a consolidated fact was produced by **merging two corroborating facts** (disjunctive — survives if one parent survives) it is indistinguishable from one produced by **joining two complementary facts** (conjunctive — must die if either parent dies). Erasing one parent then either over-deletes or under-deletes, and Art. 17 makes under-deletion the expensive failure.

**Minimal fix that buys correct cascade semantics without full `N[X]`:** store DNF instead of a flat set —
```ts
// derivedFrom as PosBool(X) in DNF: outer array = alternative derivations (+),
// inner array = jointly-required parents (×). Survives iff ∃ monomial with no erased parent.
derivedFrom: z.array(z.array(zodObjectId).min(1)).min(1).optional()
```
Or, cheaper: keep the flat array and add a discriminator `derivation: "merge" | "corroboration" | "inference" | "summary"`, with a documented per-kind cascade rule. `"corroboration"` → survive-if-any (rewrite text, drop the erased parent, recompute confidence); everything else → delete-if-any.

### 1.2 Deletion propagation is NP-hard in general — so pick your objective

**[V-snippet]** Buneman, Khanna, Tan, *On the Propagation of Deletions and Annotations through Views*, PODS 2002, pp.150–158 — https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/on-the-propagation-of-deletions-and-annotations-through-views/ · https://www.academia.edu/681183/On_Propagation_of_Deletions_and_Annotations_Through_Views

Two distinct optimisation objectives, and they conflict:
- **Source side-effect:** delete the minimum number of *input* tuples to remove view tuple $t$.
- **View side-effect:** delete input tuples so that the minimum number of *other output* tuples collaterally die.

They prove a **dichotomy**: for queries in the same class, each objective is either in P or NP-hard. **[V-snippet]** Follow-ups: *Multi-Tuple Deletion Propagation* (Kimelfeld et al.) http://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/user/dwoodruf/www/kvw13.pdf ; *New Results on the Complexity of Deletion Propagation* https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-57602-8_30 ; a 2025 unified treatment, Gatterbauer & Simons, *A unified and practical approach to Generalized Deletion Propagation* https://gatterbauer.name/download/Gatterbauer-Simons2025-Generalized-Deletion-Propagation.pdf

**Practical takeaway:** don't try to be optimal. For GDPR you are **not** solving the optimisation problem — you are solving the *forced* problem: the erasure target is given, and you must take the transitive closure. Optimality only matters if you want to minimise collateral damage to unrelated facts, and there the answer is "make your provenance finer-grained (§1.1) so there is less collateral damage by construction."

### 1.3 The AI-side equivalent: Truth Maintenance Systems

**[V]** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason_maintenance

- **JTMS** (Doyle 1979): each belief node carries **justifications** (in-list, out-list) and an `IN`/`OUT` label. A node is `IN` iff it has at least one *valid* justification. Retracting a premise flips it `OUT`, and **dependency-directed backtracking** walks only the affected sub-network rather than recomputing everything.
- **ATMS** (de Kleer 1986): each node carries a **label** = minimal set of *environments* (assumption sets) under which it holds — this is literally `Why(X)`/DNF provenance, and it lets you answer "which facts survive under which surviving sources" for all subsets at once.

**Why you care:** a JTMS is the right mental model for the nightly consolidation job. Consolidated facts are *derived nodes*; source documents are *premises*. When a premise is retracted (Art. 17), you re-label the dependency network rather than re-running consolidation from scratch. `derivedFrom` **is** the justification edge — you already have the graph, you just need the label semantics.

### 1.4 Concrete cascade algorithm for your schema

```
erasePerson(personId):
  1. FRONTIER  := sources whose PII cannot be redacted away (audio/attachments), 
                  plus facts anchored to personId
  2. Hard-delete frontier facts.
  3. FIXPOINT loop (bounded, with a visited-set to kill cycles):
       for each fact F with F.derivedFrom ∩ deletedIds ≠ ∅:
          if derivation is conjunctive  -> delete F, add to deletedIds
          if disjunctive and ∃ surviving monomial -> rewrite F.text without the
             erased parent, drop the parent id, recompute confidence, mark
             `provenanceRepaired: true`
          else -> delete F
     repeat until no change (depth cap ~8, then alert)
  4. Drop derived caches wholesale (dossiers) — cheaper and safer than surgery;
     they rebuild lazily. (You already do this. Good.)
  5. Redact retained audit artefacts (proposals) rather than deleting them.
     (You already do this. Good — see §2.4 on why retention of the audit trail
     is defensible under Art. 17(3)(e).)
  6. Flag sources with no surviving facts for blob deletion; two-phase with
     `blobsPendingDeletion` + `markSourceBlobsDeleted`. (You already do this.
     This is the correct crash-safe pattern.)
  7. Emit an append-only erasure receipt (see §2.6).
```

**Gap in the current implementation worth checking:** step 3 (transitive `derivedFrom` closure) — your `ErasureReport` reports `factsDeleted` but the consolidation job creates facts whose `derivedFrom` may reference facts anchored to *other* people while still containing the erased person's text. A merged fact "Anna and Petra both objected to the Q3 timeline" is anchored to Anna, derived from a Petra fact, and *still names Petra*. The name-token redactor handles the text, but the fact document itself survives with a dangling `derivedFrom` pointer. **Recommend:** run the redactor over `facts.text` too, and validate `derivedFrom` referential integrity post-erasure.
